Gassendi's hostile-commission and break-in details are Gassendi-only (grade C colour). The book cataloguing ('Registeret vi alle junkers bøger') stands under 21 March 1597 in the diary — on Hven, before the 11 April move; Christianson's weekday 'Saturday' for the 2 June departure is a slip (Thursday, Julian).
17 April 1597 – 20 April 1597cal. Roskilde A
othersocial visitin transit
Tycho travelled to Roskilde on Sunday 17 April 1597 — the meteorological diary records 'Profectus est Tycho Roschyldiam' — into a stormy night and next-day blizzard, in the week of the church-ordinance prosecution of his Hven pastor Jens Jensen Wensøsil, tried before Bishop Peter Winstrup on Friday 22 April with the Kronborg commander Ditlev Holck sent to 'assist'. On Wednesday 20 April he met his brothers Steen and Axel Brahe, both state councillors, presumably concerting a defence. Wensøsil was convicted on both charges — omitting exorcism, and failing to punish Tycho, 'who for eighteen years has not taken Holy Eucharist but has lived an evil life with a mistress'. The real target was Tycho himself; he still held the prebend of the Holy Three Kings chapel there, lost on 10 June to the chancellor. The diary stops abruptly on 22 April 1597, never resumed.

June 1597 Gedser C
in transitexile
At Gedser, the port on the southern tip of Denmark, the exile party took ship for the Baltic crossing to Rostock in the first half of June 1597: 'a few days later, they saw their last of Denmark. Tycho Brahe sailed away from his native land.' Most of the more than twenty travellers — Tycho, Kirsten, the six children, chaplain Wensøsil and the servants — would never see Denmark again. The embarkation point is Christianson's reconstruction; other sources have the ship taken at Copenhagen itself (Gassendi, Jonsson) or the route run via Lübeck (Norlind).

June 1597 Køge C
in transitexile
First named stage of the exile road out of Copenhagen, early June 1597: the heavy caravan of wagons — books, manuscripts, printed sheets, laboratory equipment, disassembled instruments, the great globe, ironbound chests of gold, silver and jewels, under mounted and armed escort — lumbered south along the coast road through Køge toward Vordingborg. The halt is route reconstruction, not an independently dated document; Norlind's independent reconstruction likewise runs the journey 'probably over Køge', though he then continues it via Lübeck rather than the Falster crossing.

June 1597 Nykøbing Falster C
in transitexile
Ferried across the narrow straits to Falster, the exile party rode on through Nykøbing — seat of another royal castle formerly commanded by Tycho's foster father Jørgen Brahe, the second family landmark on the southbound road — before making for the port of Gedser at the island's southern tip. Like the other Danish road stations of June 1597, this is Christianson's reconstruction of the standard southern route rather than an independently documented halt; Tycho's presence on the road between Copenhagen (2 June) and Rostock (mid-June) is itself secure.

June 1597 – 8 September 1597cal. Rostock A
exilecourt & patronagepropertysocial visit
Tycho and his familia of about twenty settled into temporary quarters in Rostock around mid-June 1597, warmly received in his old student city — Chytraeus wrote a welcoming note on 16 June, and Lucas Bacmeister still kept the house of the 1566 duel. At St Mary's he took Holy Eucharist with his family for the first time in eighteen years. On 10 July he sent Christian IV the proud Danish-language letter defending his departure and offering to continue his work 'on fair conditions'; the crushing answer, dated 8 October, reached him only at Wandsbek. He sought Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg's intercession (late July), wrote Erik Sparre on 7 September about a Baltic island from King Sigismund, and lent the young Mecklenburg dukes 10,000 daler at 12 per cent, bond dated 24 August, secured on Amt Doberan — he had not left Denmark impoverished. Plague striking the town, he accepted Rantzau's Holstein invitation and left on 8 September 1597. Sent originals to Moritz of Hesse-Kassel (17 July) and Sparre (7 September) anchor presence.

in transitexile

Christianson stages here Tycho's meditation on exiled kinsmen who returned in honour: Peter Oxe, his brother Knud Brahe, Erik Sparre, Erik Lange. September 1597 – 8 October 1597 (bounds uncertain) Bramstedt B
court & patronagesocial visit
From Segeberg Tycho and the familia proceeded to Bramstedt, where Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau received them with open arms in the second half of September 1597. Host and guest — two of the most famous learned aristocrats of the North, friends since Tycho's Rostock student days — talked over patronage strategy and a suitable residence until a Danish restoration could be won. Under the delicate protocol of status Rantzau would not become Tycho's patron nor Tycho his client; as friend and equal he offered, of the eighteen castles and manors he and his sons owned, Wandsburg near Hamburg, over the head of its lessee Georg Ludwig Frobenius, Tycho's old Hven acquaintance. Thoren has Tycho still (or again) at Bramstedt on 8 October 1597, talking over the alternatives when he sent a letter to Basel.

c. 8 September 1597 – September 1597 Doberan C
in transitproperty
Leaving Rostock on 8 September 1597, the Brahe caravan proceeded westward through Doberan on the coastal road toward Wismar and Holstein — a pointed waypoint, since the whole Amt of Doberan had just been pledged as surety for Tycho's 10,000-daler loan to the young Mecklenburg dukes. Having refused to pay the sum out at Wismar, Tycho had offered to deliver it at Doberan in person, 'which probably happened' in Norlind's hedged wording; Friis, however, records only the promise, never the execution — and in 1601 it was Eske Bille and his servant, not Tycho, who travelled to Doberan and Rostock for the repayment. The passage is a named route stage in Christianson; no halt or business is independently documented.

17 September 1597 Segeberg A
in transitcourt & patronageexile
By 17 September 1597 the exile party had reached Segeberg fortress, seat of Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau's administration of royal Schleswig-Holstein — one of the castles Rantzau had offered — only to find the viceroy away at Bramstedt. From Segeberg Tycho wrote him the dated letter (TBOO VIII,5) that fixes his presence: the castle pleased him, but he had left Hven to relocate, not retire — he had books to finish and needed typographic equipment, engravers and printers, so he asked for a residence near a city like Hamburg or Lübeck and offered to come to Bramstedt to discuss plans. That criterion shortly selected Wandsburg. Thoren's 'first estate, too remote for his taste', from which the 17 September letter was sent, is this same station, not a separate unnamed castle.

October 1597 – 29 September 1598cal. Wandsbek A
exilebooks & printingcourt & patronageobservationinstrumentsalchemy & medicine
A year as Rantzau's guest — not client — at the moated castle of Wandsburg in Wandsbek on Hamburg's outskirts, living in quasi-princely style, honoured at church in a special loge. Christian IV's rebuff of 8 October 1597 reached him here; on 20 October he entered the account of his interrupted observations and composed the Elegia ad Daniam, and on 21 October resumed observing, at first with only a radius, from February 1598 with quadrants, sextant and armilla (pole height 53°36'; lunar eclipse 10 February with Rosenkrantz assisting, solar eclipse 25 February, lunar 6 August). His own press from Hven, worked by the Hamburg printer Philipp von Ohr, produced the Astronomiae instauratae mechanica (dedication to Rudolf II dated 31 December 1597, ready early 1598), while copyists lettered vellum exemplars of the 1,000-star catalogue; both went out to princes and scholars across Europe as the patronage suit which, brokered by Rantzau, Hagecius, Corraducius and the Elector of Cologne, produced the imperial invitation in the summer. He kept a laboratory, shared medical recipes with Rantzau, answered Kepler's Mysterium on 1 April 1598, and received a stream of Danish students, Müller, Fabricius and, from August 1598, Longomontanus. Day-dated letters and album leaves run from 2 January to 14 September 1598. Just after Michaelmas, 29 September 1598, the caravan rolled out toward the Elbe road.

22 December 1597 Bramstedt A
court & patronagesocial visit
Viceroy Rantzau arranged for Tycho to meet Margrave Joachim Frederick of Brandenburg and Margravine Catherine of Brandenburg-Küstrin at Bramstedt on 22 December 1597, as the parents of Christian IV's bride returned home through Holstein from the royal wedding (Haderslev, 27 November). Tycho handed the margrave a letter and memorandum of his reasons for leaving Denmark, seeking intercession with his new royal son-in-law — either the permanent endowment of Uraniborg or leave to remove the four great instruments with compensation. The accommodating couple's letters to king and queen of January–February 1598 (25 January and days following) led to nothing. The meeting also renewed acquaintance with the Brandenburg court astrologer Johannes Müller, who had visited Hven in 1596 and would shortly join Tycho at Wandsbek.

October 1598 – December 1598 (bounds uncertain)cal. Dresden A
in transitcourt & patronage
Tycho, his sons, Tengnagel and a small suite spent about a month in the Electoral Saxon residence city (late October to the first days of December 1598). He announced his approach to the imperial court through Vice-Chancellor Corraducius; the round trip of the inquiry took a month, Prague being gripped by plague and Rudolf withdrawn (to Pilsen, per Björklund's Bilag 4). Secretary Barvitius's reply — the emperor was pleased he was on the way but he should wait at a safe distance — turned him to wintering at Wittenberg. In Dresden he had an audience with Duke Frederick William of Saxe-Altenburg, administrator of Electoral Saxony, presenting illuminated copies of the Mechanica and star catalogue to the duke, the boy Elector Christian II and Chancellor Mosbach, and receiving a golden chain with three portrait medallions worth over 130 gulden. From Dresden on 28 November 1598 he dated the letter to the Doge of Venice — carried by Tengnagel across the Alps, proposing among other things the affiliate observatory at Alexandria — and wrote Magini after a seven-year silence. His son Tycho was sent back to Wandsbek to fetch the family.

October 1598 Magdeburg A
in transitcourt & patronagepropertysocial visit
The caravan progressed up the Elbe to Magdeburg and halted about eight days in October 1598. Tycho met his long-time correspondent Rector Georg Rollenhagen — source of the first warnings of Ursus's plagiarism and of imperial-court intelligence via Caspar Lehmann, including the rumour that Rudolf meant to grant him Brandeis castle. Erik Lange, Sophie Brahe's absconded betrothed, turned up: Tycho barred him and his gold-making schemes from the Prague party, but before a summoned notary required his sworn public testimony on Ursus's 1584 conduct at Uraniborg — ammunition for the plagiarism war. Strategy changed here: the heavy instruments and baggage were stored at Magdeburg (they stayed until 1600), and Longomontanus escorted Kirsten and the daughters back to Wandsburg — prospects being too uncertain to drag the whole household on — while Tycho, his sons, Tengnagel and a few others pressed on toward Dresden.

5 October 1598 Harburg A
in transitcourt & patronage
First call of the Prague journey: the caravan — three splendid carriages, Tycho's drawn by six horses, out of Wandsburg just after Michaelmas — crossed to the ducal seat of Harburg on the Elbe's south bank, where Tycho paid his respects to the aged Duke Otto II of Braunschweig-Lüneburg, whose daughter Duchess Elisabeth was married to Tycho's Swedish kinsman Count Erik Brahe. He presented an illuminated copy of the Mechanica bound in green silk, inscribed 5 October 1598; the fascinated duke asked for his nativity and reciprocated with a letter of recommendation to the imperial High Steward Wolfgang Rumpf — a document Tycho would produce at his Prague audience the next summer, alongside the commendations of Elector Ernest and Duke Ulrich.

25 October 1598 Wittenberg A
in transit
A dated album leaf — 'Suspiciendo despicio', Tycho's personal device (Sotheby's Paris, 15 December 2004, lot 36) — places him bodily at Wittenberg on 25 October 1598, between the Magdeburg week and the Dresden month. The Elbe road from Magdeburg to Dresden passed through Wittenberg, where, per Thoren, the Jessenius acquaintance was first made in passing; the leaf is therefore read as a transit attestation on the outward leg, not the start of the winter residence, which the biographies date from 4 December. A candidate host album, Johann Nesen's Stammbuch (Zittau, Christian-Weise-Bibliothek B 178, the Tycho leaf excised), records the entry under 26 October 1598 — a one-day discrepancy unresolved. An undated 1598 Wittenberg entry now trimmed into the Merseburg autograph collection belongs either to this passage or to the December residence.

4 December 1598 – 14 June 1599cal. Wittenberg A
exileeducationbooks & printingobservationalchemy & medicinesocial visit
Tycho and his sons arrived in Wittenberg on 4 December 1598 and lodged with the anatomist Johannes Jessenius (Jan Jesenský) in Philipp Melanchthon's former house — later Caspar Peucer's, known to Tycho from his 1566 student days. He set up a chemical laboratory on the ground floor, observed the sun's meridian altitude on 9 December, and gathered a circle including the mathematician Melchior Jöstelius (who perfected prosthaphaeresis with him), the theologian Ägidius Hunnius and the poet Friedrich Taubmann. The total lunar eclipse of 31 January 1599 ran nearly half an hour against his lunar theory, halting the Progymnasmata Moon-section printing for recalculation — a manuscript ephemeris for 1599 was substituted as imperial gift. In February 1599, never before formally matriculated, he enrolled with his sons and famulus Johannes Eriksen; the rector feted him at the castle. Kirsten and the daughters, from Wandsburg 6 January, arrived mid-January. Coraduz's summons matured through the spring, but carriage horses, Magdalene's grave illness, thaw and floods delayed departure until 14 June 1599 — the farewell album leaf 'quo Witebergā discessi'. The densest dated-autograph run of his life spans the stay: 14 January (Hagecius Mechanica dedication), 28 February (his son's album), 6 March (Sinnich), 16 April (the Palingenius leaf, Sophia stock 6196), 8 and 29 May.

The sources disagree. Arrival: 4 December 1598 (Christianson p.302, Norlind p.298; Dreyer 'first week of December') vs the internal stores' c.21 October back-calculation from a 236-day figure and Nielsen's 'Oct 1598' interlude start — 4 December followed, the 25 October leaf read as an en-route touch. Departure: 'at Easter 1599' (Nielsen; Dreyer and Friis 'shortly after Easter'; Gassendi 'not before Easter, for the floods') vs the dated leaves of 16 April, 8 and 29 May and the 14 June 1599 farewell self-dating (Christianson, Norlind) — 14 June governs. Length: Jessenius's funeral oration says nine months; the documented span is about six and a half; the stores' 236-day figure (implying October arrival) is unexplained. Cause of the halt: plague at Prague and the scattered court (all biographies, Gassendi, Jonsson) vs Šíma-Valeška's express rejection of the plague explanation — the plague account is far better attested but the objection is flagged. Calendar of 14 June: Thoren 'corrects Norlind' toward old style, yet Norlind's own text prints '14 juni 1599 g.st.' — an extraction-level discrepancy, both in fact Julian. Family logistics: women from Wandsburg 6 January, arrived mid-January (Christianson) vs Dreyer's 'escorted by Longomontanus as far as Magdeburg, joined during the winter' vs Friis's separate route 'via Magdeburg to Dresden'. Dreyer additionally has the post-Easter departure leave the family 'half way, at Dresden' — against Christianson's 14 June departure 'with all his familia'; the day-dated leaf governs, the Dresden family-parking belongs, if real, to the 1599 journey (p8).

Bohemia

1599–1601

The Bohemian climax. Summoned by Rudolf II, Tycho left Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 and travelled via Pretzsch and Dresden to Prague, where a wholly private imperial audience made him court astronomer at 3,000 gulden a year. Choosing Benátky nad Jizerou over Brandeis and Lysá, he built his last observatory there from August 1599, received Kepler in February 1600, and fled plague to Girsitz over the winter. Recalled to Prague in June 1600, he lodged at the Golden Griffin, set his twenty-eight instruments up at the Belvedere, and moved into the Curtius house in February 1601. The Rožmberk banquet of 13 October 1601 began the fatal illness; he died on 24 October and was buried in the Týn Church on 4 November.

c. 1599 Lysá nad Labem B
in transitproperty
Inspection waypoint of the Bohemian settlement search. Offered the choice among the imperial castles of Lysá, Brandeis and Benátky 'zur Exercirung seines Studii', Tycho was driven around to view them all before choosing Benátky — Friis states expressly that he was conducted to all three. Nothing further is recorded of the Lysá visit itself; the viewing falls between the July 1599 audience and the removal to Benátky of 20-21 August.

June 1599 – August 1599cal. Prague A
court & patronageexileobservationinstruments
Arrival in Bohemia and the making of the imperial appointment. Reaching Prague in late June or the first days of July 1599 — Ursus fleeing the city at his approach — Tycho was greeted by the privy secretary Barvitius, received by High Steward Rumpf in long Latin conversation, and granted a wholly private audience by Rudolf II, who took his hand, accepted the three presentation volumes (the Mechanica, the vellum star catalogue, the sun-and-moon theory) and promised 3,000 gulden yearly with a hereditary fief to follow. He was lodged in the late vice-chancellor Curtius's house on Hradčany, where a painted pedestal in the Uraniborg manner was built; he signed the von Wicken album at Prague on 13 July; he observed the 22 July solar eclipse with his own instruments while his assistant watched from the Carolinum tower, and his Prague solar series ends 31 July. Finding the Curtius tower too small and dreading visitors, he asked for a country seat and was offered three castles.

14 June 1599 – 15 June 1599cal. Pretzsch A
in transitsocial visit
First halt of the definitive move to Bohemia. Leaving Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 with the whole familia — a train of wagons, carriages and outriders — Tycho spent the first evening at Castle Pretzsch on the Elbe as guest of the Saxon hereditary marshal Johann (Hans) Löser, a courtesy the recently money-humbled astronomer thought worth recording for Rosenkrantz. The party continued upriver toward Dresden the next day.

16 June 1599 – June 1599cal. Dresden A
in transitfamily
The Dresden split of the household. Arriving on 16 June 1599, two days out of Wittenberg, Tycho left Kirsten, the daughters and their servants in the care of Johann Tauchmann, a high Saxon court official and brother-in-law of his Wittenberg collaborator Jöstelius, and went on toward Prague in his finest carriage with his sons and Claus Mule — a deliberate strategy of appearing before the emperor unencumbered, and of holding a line of retreat. On imperial instructions after the first audience the family was fetched, reaching Prague eight days after being sent for.

20 August 1599 – June 1600 (bounds uncertain)cal. Benátky nad Jizerou A · site record →
observationinstrumentsalchemy & medicinecourt & patronagefamilyproperty
The last observatory. Choosing Benátky nad Jizerou — highest of the three offered crown estates, c. 35 km northeast of Prague above the 'Venice of Bohemia' — Tycho arrived about 20-21 August 1599, had his first instrument mounted by 28 August, and set about remodelling the castle into a new Uraniborg with observatory and chymical laboratory, against the obstruction of the administrator Mühlstein and an empty treasury (imperial resolution of 10 December 1599: 1,000 gulden yearly from the Brandeis-Benátky rents). His first recorded observation there is 11 September 1599; datelines run 'from the imperial castle Benatky' from 7 September 1599 to 15 May 1600. Son Tycho and Claus Mule fetched the great instruments from Denmark; Longomontanus rejoined in January 1600 for the lunar theory; Kepler first met him here on 3 February 1600 and was set to Mars, the contract quarrel mediated by Jessenius on 5 April. David Gans came thrice from Prague, five days each. Observations break off at the end of June 1600, when the emperor recalled him to Prague.

The sources disagree. Departure for Prague: observations end at the end of June 1600 (Studnicka; Christianson 2020 has the household leave after Rudolf's 10 June return) vs early July (Norlind) vs c. August on Barvitius's advice (Dreyer); June followed as the modern consensus, with Friis's dateline gap (15 May 1600 Benátky - 26 September 1600 Prague) bracketing it. Kepler's arrival: 3 February 1600 (Dreyer, McEvoy in Crossroads) vs 4 February summons (Christianson 2020) vs 'January to Prague' (Jönsson, outlier) — 3 February followed. Longomontanus's discharge: 18 July 1600 at Benátky (Christianson 2000) vs 4 August / August 1600 (Christianson 2020, Friis, Norlind, Dreyer). The Hamburg-senate letter's two internal datings (29 Sep 1599 slug vs '27 jan. n.s. Benatky') disagree; both place Tycho at Benátky in 1599-1600. Jönsson places Benátky 'southwest' of Prague — a geographical error; the castle lies northeast.
20 August 1599 – 21 August 1599cal. Brandýs nad Labem A
in transitproperty
Seen on the castle-selection circuit and passed over — sitting low, the Emperor's favourite hunting-lodge — Brandeis nonetheless anchors the removal to Benátky: on the way there Tycho datelined a letter to Longomontanus at Rostock from Brandeis, 20 August 1599 (new style), reporting a level road about six hours from Prague and that an official of Brandeis would carry him and all his effects to Benátky that day or the next. Brandeis remained the administrative seat, under Kaspar von Mühlstein, from which his Benátky building funds were grudgingly managed. He never resided here.

November 1599 – January 1600 Girsitz (Jičice?) B
otherobservationin transit
Plague refuge. After two thousand deaths in the Benátky district — a travelling companion of the visiting cousin Claus Steensen Bille sickened and died on arrival — Tycho took the frightened household to the castle of Girsitz in the first half of November 1599. He said they stayed six or seven weeks: his first letter from Girsitz is of 16 November, the last officially sent from there of 31 December 1599, with the return to Benátky in the new year; some intervening letters were addressed from Benátky 'just to avoid complicating things', so the exact return is unfixable. Some observations were made in December, and during this visitation the Emperor asked Tycho for the prescription of his elixir against epidemic diseases.

Duration: Christianson confines the refuge to November-December 1599; Thoren and Norlind extend the return into the new year — the 31 December last letter supports a January 1600 return.

c. April 1600 Prague B
social visitin transit
The Kepler reconciliation. About three weeks after Kepler's angry departure from Benátky on 6 April 1600 and his withdrawal to Baron Hoffmann's house in Prague, Hoffmann's and Jessenius's mediation and Kepler's repentant letter brought the two astronomers together at Prague: Tycho drove into the city — something he had told Kepler he did not like to do — was reconciled with his errant assistant, and fetched him back to Benátky, where Kepler worked a further four weeks before leaving for Graz at the beginning of June.

c. 1 May 1600 Prague A
social visit
At the beginning of May 1600, while resident at Benátky, Tycho attended Caspar von Mühlstein's wedding in Prague — a sign of cordial relations with the estates' captain after the December 1599 settlement of their funding frictions. Tycho's own letter of 15 May 1600 dates it: 'wie ich fur 14 tage zu Prage, auf des Herrn Haubtmans von Brandeis Hochzeit gewesen'. In this period he grew acquainted with Protestant aristocrats including Baron Ehrenfried von Minckwitz, who blazoned the same arms as his Ulfstand grandmother, and Baron Siegfried von Rindscheid, the alchemist who had visited Uraniborg with Erik Lange in 1584.

June 1600 – 24 October 1601 (bounds uncertain)cal. Prague A
court & patronageobservationbooks & printingfamilyinstrumentsdeath & burial
The final residence. Summoned when Rudolf II returned from Pilsen on 10 June 1600, Tycho moved to Prague suddenly and permanently: first weeks in the noisy Golden Griffin inn on Nový Svět below the castle (twice summoned to the palace in one day), then a private house near Baron Hoffmann's by the Loreto square. The twenty-eight instruments — from Benátky, and the great ones from Hven via the Magdeburg transit dispute — arrived by October-November 1600 and were installed at the Belvedere; the press resumed the Progymnasmata; Jacob Monaw brought the Wittich library's annotated De revolutionibus copies in October 1600, and Kepler, expelled from Styria, returned destitute on 19 October 1600 and was set to refuting Ursus. On 25 February 1601 the household moved into the Curtius house, bought by the emperor. Elisabeth married Tengnagel on 17 June 1601; in September 1601 Tycho presented Kepler to the emperor and the Tabulae Rudolphinae were named. His last observation is dated 11 October 1601; the Rožmberk banquet of 13 October began the fatal illness, and he died at home on 24 October 1601, aged 54 years 10 months, charging Kepler to complete the tables in the Tychonic scheme.

The sources disagree. Start of the permanent Prague residence: June 1600 on Rudolf's 10 June return (Thoren, Christianson 2000/2020, Jönsson) vs 'about the beginning of July' (Norlind, from the 3 August postscript 'called a month ago') vs 'about August' (Dreyer) — June followed (modern consensus); Friis's datelines bracket it 15 May - 26 September 1600, his 26 July 'In eil, Prag' letter possibly the move itself. Death date: 24 October 1601 unanimous against Kepler's '24 November' slip (Gassendi's refutation) and the older '13 October old style' (Studnicka's correction: 13 October n.s. is the banquet). Time of death: 'around nine that evening' (Christianson 2020) vs 'between nine and ten in the forenoon' (Jönsson) vs morning (Friis, Dreyer) — morning better attested. Elisabeth's wedding: 17 June 1601 (Thoren, Jönsson, Christianson) vs Friis's 'between Easter and Pentecost 1601'. Cause of death: uraemia from prostatic hypertrophy (Norlind; modern opinion per Thoren; Christianson via Jessenius) vs the contemporary stone attribution (Wittich; no stones found at exhumation); per the Debunked Claims Register, mercury poisoning is excluded by the 2010 exhumation and uraemia is consistent but unproven — Christianson 2000's 'body heavy with quicksilver from Paracelsian elixirs' is not carried as fact. Norlind judges the Capuchin-protocol account of Tycho's court role 'extremely tendentious and certainly historically false in most points'.
2 December 1600 – February 1601 (bounds uncertain)cal. Prague B · site record →
observationinstruments
Surrogate Uraniborg. In the Royal Summer Palace of Queen Anna — the Belvedere, 'non longe ab Arce in Caesaris quadam magnifice exstructa domo' in Tycho's report of 24 January 1601 — his twenty-eight instruments, arrived in Prague in October–November 1600 (Thoren: sometime in October, a few weeks after the Magdeburg consignment), were stored and mounted on the second-storey porch, and on 2 December 1600 the observations broken off at Benátky at the end of June were resumed; by Christmas night Tycho was observing. Pierre Bergeron (1607) records that the great Danish mathematician made his precise observations in the ground-floor arcaded galleries — reported rather than firmly documented for Tycho's own person. After his death the building housed the astronomical section of Rudolf's collections, a memorial musaeum with two portraits of Tycho.

25 February 1601 – 24 October 1601cal. Prague A · site record →
court & patronageobservationfamilydeath & burial
Last workplace and deathplace. On 25 February 1601 the familia moved into the refurbished summer palace of the late vice-chancellor Jacob Kurz von Senftenau (Curtius) on Hradčany, bought by the emperor for 10,000 thaler and transformed toward a 'New Imperial Uraniborg'; observing resumed there on 3 March 1601, seven teams having taken the solar culmination simultaneously on 28 February. Elisabeth Brahe married Tengnagel in the house in June 1601; the Pruskowski Mechanica dedication of 12 March 1601, among the latest securely-dated Tycho autographs, was signed in this residence. After the banquet of 13 October Tycho returned here unable to pass water and died on 24 October 1601, Kirsten, Kepler and the household about him, Longomontanus and Tengnagel far from Prague. The Bohemian royal astronomer Alois David fixed the observation tower's coordinates in 1803; the structure was demolished in 1804.

13 October 1601cal. Prague A · site record →
social visit
The fatal banquet. On 13 October 1601 Tycho went with the councillor Ehrenfried von Minckwitz to dine at the palace of Petr Vok z Rožmberka — by Thoren's reckoning (Appendix 5) the Renaissance palace on Hradčany square later known as the Schwarzenberg palace — a magnate of his bookish Prague circle, owner of some 10,000 books and manuscripts. Forbearing, as manners required while his host remained at table, to rise and relieve himself, he held his urine too long; by the time he returned home he could not urinate, and the eleven-day fatal illness began. The retention story is the contemporary tradition transmitted by Kepler's log and the funeral oration, not an established medical fact.

4 November 1601cal. Prague A · site record →
death & burial
The burial. On 4 November 1601 a solemn procession bore the coffin — velvet-covered, hung with his ancestors' gilded arms, preceded by the black damask banner with his title, his led horse and gilt rapier — across the Charles Bridge along the royal way to the Church of Our Lady before Týn in the Old Town, where the utraquist rite still allowed a Protestant service. Twelve noble imperial guardsmen carried him; his younger son Jørgen walked between Count Erik Brahe and Baron von Minckwitz, the widow following; the eldest son and son-in-law Tengnagel were abroad. Jessenius delivered the funeral oration, printed at Prague the same year. The red Slivenec marble monument — armoured effigy, hand on the celestial globe, 'NON FASCES, NEC OPES, SOLA ARTIS SCEPTRA PERENNANT' — still marks the tomb, where Kirsten was laid beside him in 1604. (This final entry records the burial rite of 4 November — Tycho died on 24 October; it closes the itinerary as the body's last journey, not a living presence.)

The gazetteer, grouped by region and ordered by first arrival: each place with its period names, its pin (or an honest “not mappable”), every documented stay, and — for Hven, Prague and Benátky — the site records beneath it.

Scania

Knutstorp castle-manor A 6 documented stays
Knutstorp Castle (Knutstorps borg), near Kågeröd, Scania, Sweden · period names: Knudstrup, Knudstorpium, Knutstorp, curia Knusdorpiana · 55.9400, 13.0900
Brahe family seat in then-Danish Scania and Tycho's birthplace; he was styled 'til Knudstrup' in every chancery entry, co-holding with his brother Steen.
The manor of Tycho's birth was replaced in 1551 by the surviving red-brick building (Thoren).
c. 14 December 1546 – 1548cal. A
family
Tycho Brahe was born at his family's ancestral seat of Knutstorp in Scania on 14 December 1546, between nine and ten in the morning by his father Otte Brahe's own memorandum; the Stephanius notes, copied from Tycho's lost self-horoscope, give 10:47 a.m. The firstborn of twins — his brother was stillborn, later the subject of his first publication (1572) — he was baptised Tyge after his paternal grandfather, Latinising the name at university. Norlind and Thoren place the birth in the medieval manor that preceded the moated brick castle Otte built from 1551. He remained with his parents Otte Brahe and Beate Bille only until about mid-1548, when, after the birth of his brother Steen (21 December 1547), his childless uncle Jørgen Brahe carried him off, 'without the knowledge of my parents', to raise as his own. Knutstorp remained his lifelong territorial designation.

Birth building: Norlind and Thoren argue the medieval manor, not the 1551 castle of the later tradition.
c. June 1565 – April 1566 B
familyproperty
About a year at home in Denmark between the Leipzig and Wittenberg residences, June 1565 to April 1566, bracketed by the Stephanius notes (Rostock 25 May 1565; 'returned to Wittenberg on April 15, 1566, from his fatherland'). Jørgen Brahe's death on 21 June 1565 changed Tycho's status: the plan to make him heir to Tostrup lapsed, and Inger Oxe, widowed, continued to regard him 'with a quite special love'. He recorded no observations that year, occupied himself with ordering his money matters and gathering funds for the peregrination he had resolved on, and found the nobility's contempt for his studies galling — of his relations only Steen Bille approved. By spring 1566 he had won leave, or simply asserted himself, to depart.

1571 – 1575 (bounds uncertain) A
propertyfamilyobservation
The family seat anchored Tycho's Scanian years: he and his brother Steen co-inherited Knutstorp at Otte Brahe's death, both styling themselves 'of Knudstrup' for life, while their mother Beate Bille kept dower occupancy. Here she revealed his stillborn twin, prompting the Latin elegy printed in 1572 as his first publication; here he formed his union with Kirsten Jorgensdatter, their first daughter born in October 1573. The De nova stella preface is dated 'Knusdorp', 5 May 1573; an ague kept him home that summer. On 8 December 1573 he observed the lunar eclipse foretold in his book with the new gilt-brass quadrant, assisted by his sister Sophie - his own note records 'Hanc ego Eclipsin in curia mea Knusdorpiana observavi diligenter'. Settlement of the paternal estate ran to spring 1575, from which he drew about 650 dalers a year.

c. December 1575 – February 1576 A
propertyfamily
Home about the end of 1575, Tycho made Knutstorp his base for the winter, secretly resolved to sell his share of the estate, buy property at Basel and leave Denmark for good - lying awake, in Christianson's phrase, wondering how he could escape. The Soro, Copenhagen and Herrevad consultations of the following weeks all radiated from this base. In the early dawn of 11 February 1576, before he had risen from bed, a royal page who had ridden through the night was brought to his bedside with Frederik II's command to attend him in Zealand at once - the summons that ended the Basel plan and opened the road to Hven. The summons and its sequel belong to the next period.

10 February 1576 – 16 February 1576 A
familycourt & patronage
Tycho lay awake at Knutstorp planning how to slip away to Basel without alerting his relatives when, about two hours before dawn on 11 February 1576, a royal courier who had ridden all night arrived commanding him to the king at Ibstrup. He returned to Knutstorp the next day, 12 February, to contemplate the offer of Hven, struck that the courier had come at the very moment of his escape plan. From here he wrote the long letter to Pratensis describing the audience, consulted his mother, brother Steen and Kirsten, then rode out to Herrevad and Copenhagen before accepting at Frederiksborg on the 18th.

3 September 1576 A
propertysocial visit
A Latin letter written from Knudstrup on 3 September 1576 to the royal physician Peder Sorensen (Severinus) offers to pay for a monument to the recently dead Johannes Pratensis if Sorensen will compose the inscription; the monument was erected in Frue Kirke, Copenhagen. Document-grade evidence that Tycho was at his half-inherited family seat weeks after Uraniborg's foundation stone was laid - the dateline pair with the 21 November letter from 'Our Island of Hven' fixes the shift of his base onto the island during the first building season's autumn.

Tosterup castle-manor B 1 documented stay
Tosterup Castle, near Tomelilla, Scania, Sweden · period names: Tosterup, Tostrup · 55.5500, 13.9700
Jørgen Brahe's ancestral seat in eastern Scania, Tycho's foster 'home' per the core biographies; the danish-context package notes its own sources never place the upbringing here. In then-Danish Scania (Danish until 1658).
c. 1548 – April 1559 B
familyeducation
The fostered boyhood was based at Jørgen Brahe's ancestral seat of Tostrup in eastern Scania, where the childless Jørgen and Inger Oxe raised him as their only charge, with visits to Knutstorp to see his birth parents. From about his seventh year (c. 1553) he was put to Latin and the rudiments of learning — Dreyer and Friis with a private tutor (Hovmester) in the uncle's house, five years of schooling above all in Latin, in which he was soon writing letters and verse. Against the Brahe military tradition, Jørgen intended him for learned studies and a chancery career, and paid for his education until age eighteen. Friis, Norlind and Jönsson all hedge the Tostrup placement as inference from Jørgen's fief-holding; Thoren states it plainly. The stay, interleaved with residence at Jørgen's successive royal fiefs, closed when the boy was sent to the University of Copenhagen in April 1559.

Helsingborg town A 5 documented stays
Helsingborg, Scania, Sweden · period names: Helsingborg, Hälsingborg, Helsingborg Slot · 56.0465, 12.6945
Scanian castle-town opposite Elsinore, Danish until 1658; Otte Brahe's last seat as governor (d. here 1571). Tycho observed at Helsingborg on 30 December 1570; his family lived in the town 1576-77. Joensson, alone among the sources, never expressly places Tycho in the town.
The Maria Church holds the epitaph for Tycho's daughter Kirstine (d. 1576).
c. June 1565 B
observationin transit
Travelling home through Scania in June 1565, Tycho stopped at Helsingborg — the natural landfall of the Sound crossing — and made a determination of the local latitude, the first of three such stops (Helsingborg, Malmö, Knutstorp) that constitute his earliest recorded geodetic-astronomical fieldwork on home ground, made with the instruments and habits acquired at Leipzig. The stop rests on the pole-height list in his oldest observation journal, which Norlind reads as the itinerary of the journey itself.

30 December 1570 – 9 May 1571cal. A
familyobservation
The Wanderjahre's terminus: summoned home with his brothers as their father's health failed, Tycho was at Helsingborg Castle — Otte Brahe's seat as governor — by the end of 1570; Thoren has him home probably by the time the Stettin peace was concluded (13 December, the eve of his 24th birthday). The first documented trace is an observation of 30 December 1570 from the castle (Venus and Jupiter per Dreyer; the journals cited at X, 37), made with one of the cross-staffs that were the only instruments he still possessed — the same season the treaty ending the war was signed. Otte, who had called his sons home and compiled a legal listing of his estate, was bedridden by spring and died on 9 May 1571 after a severe three-day ague, aged 53, his family around the bed; Tycho poured out his grief in the letter to Vedel of 18 May 1571. Knutstorp passed jointly to Tycho and Steen; burial was at Kågeröd church.

The sources disagree. First home observation: the journals' 30 December 1570 entry (Dreyer, Friis, Norlind — archival, X, 37) against Christianson 2020's Moon observation 'at the solstice on the eve of his 24th birthday' (~13 December) and Thoren's 'by Christmas' — the 30 December anchor is followed for the documented date; arrival by mid-December remains possible per Thoren. Gassendi dated the homecoming to 1571 with a Copenhagen landfall and court salute — rejected on the strength of the 30 December 1570 Helsingborg observations (Norlind). Motive for the return: the father's grave illness (Friis, Jönsson, Håkansson 'probably') is doubted by Norlind, who notes the unhurried route and that Otte died only in May 1571. | Gassendi has Tycho returning from Augsburg only in 1571; Norlind (p. 28) refutes this with the Helsingborg observation of 30 December 1570 (TBOO X, 37) - Norlind followed. Deathbed attendance is presumption, not documented in these sources.
May 1571 – 1575 (bounds uncertain) C
familyproperty
Tycho owned town houses in Helsingborg, below the castle his father had commanded until 1571, and Kirsten Jorgensdatter probably lived in one of them - 'formodligen periodvis ensam' in Hakansson's phrase - while Tycho spent ever more time at Herrevad. Christianson suggests it was perhaps in Helsingborg that he gave her the keys to larder, cabinets and doors, the act which under Danish common law made an openly cohabiting commoner a binding morganatic wife after three winters. The daughters Kirstine (b. 1573) and Magdalene (b. 1574) were raised there; little Kirstine died of plague in the town on 24 September 1576 and was buried in the Maria church, where Tycho's Latin epitaph for her survives. Tycho's own stays in the house are implied by the household, not documented.

familydeath & burialin transit
Until September 1576 Tycho probably commuted to Hven from Helsingborg, where Kirsten and the children were living. That month an epidemic sweeping from Copenhagen into Skane carried off his eldest daughter Kirstine, not quite three; Tycho buried her in the church at Helsingborg and commissioned the bronze plaque, still in the church wall, recording her as his filiola naturalis who lived two years, eleven months, eleven days and eleven hours. For safety he took little Magdalene and the pregnant Kirsten out of the town and lodged them with the noble widow Margrethe Gagge at Tagalycka manor.

observation
During the comet of October 1580 Tycho notes in his own observation record that he observed it at Helsingborg from 20 to 27 October, while on Hven it was observed by 'Petrus and Paulus' - Peder Jakobsen Flemlose and the visiting Wroclaw mathematician Paul Wittich, working with a quadrant while Tycho used a radius across the Sound. A week's documented absence from the island, and a rare instance of Tycho conducting coordinated parallel observations from the mainland during the Hven decades; the town lay in the len whose Kulla farms he then held.

Herrevad Abbey abbey-church A 3 documented stays
Herrevad Abbey (Herrevadskloster), near Ljungbyhed, Scania, Sweden · period names: Herrevad Kloster, Herritzvadium, Herridtzvad Kloster, Herresvad · 56.0800, 13.2300
Former Cistercian abbey held in fief by Steen Bille, a few kilometres from Knutstorp; Tycho's base in the early 1570s and the site of the new-star discovery of 11 November 1572. In then-Danish Scania (Danish until 1658).
The discovery site is marked by a memorial plaque (Joensson).
1571 – 1575 (bounds uncertain) A
alchemy & medicineobservationinstrumentsfamily
From late 1571 Tycho lived mainly with his maternal uncle Steen Bille, who held the secularised Cistercian abbey of Herrevad and ran it as a proto-industrial seat: glassworks with Italian blowers, the first paper mill in Skane (which Tycho helped build), the Eket ironworks, smiths and cabinetmakers. Bille fitted out a chemical laboratory for him outside the abbey wall, and chemistry absorbed him wholly - not a single astronomical observation survives between 30 December 1570 and November 1572. On the evening of 11 November 1572, walking from the laboratory to supper, he saw the brilliant new star in Cassiopeia near the zenith, confirmed it by servants and passing peasants, and measured its distances through the winter with the newly finished walnut sextant built by the abbey's craftsmen, proving it beyond parallax - the observations published in De nova stella (1573) that redirected his life.

March 1574 – May 1574 A
observation
A documented observing run at Herrevad in the spring of 1574, part of the Skane-Oresund circuit recorded in Tycho's own observation books: chiefly distance-measures of planets from fixed stars with the sextant, 'satis exquisite, subtracta instrumenti parallaxi', a small quadrant also mentioned. The 1746 compiler of Danske Magazin, reading the manuscript observation books, names March and April; Dreyer, from the same books, extends the run into May, after which Tycho removed to Copenhagen for the rest of the year.

February 1576 A
social visitcourt & patronage
In the days after the Ibstrup audience Tycho rode to Herrevad Abbey to discuss the king's proposal with his uncle Steen Bille, who had himself acted as a broker of patronage in shaping it. The consultation weighed the abandoned alternative squarely: with Peder Oxe dead since October 1575, selling his half of Knutstorp to fund a Basel establishment would entangle his mother and brother, and refusing the king's generosity would reflect on all his relations. Herrevad was the first stop of a deliberate circuit - Herrevad, then Copenhagen - before Tycho resolved to accept Hven.

The sources disagree. Christianson followed (archival, Tycho's own account); Thoren's earlier dating preserved here.

20 July 1584 A
court & patronageproperty
As Prince Christian was hailed as future king in each province in the summer of 1584, Tycho appeared at Lund on 20 July among the entire nobility of Skane and swore the solemn oath of loyalty, followed by representatives of clergy, burghers and peasants, the long ceremony closing with a festive banquet. Dreyer links to this period the curious unexecuted draft act dated 'Huenae in Autopoli Vranopyrgensi', 1 July 1584, by which the king would have granted Hven to Tycho and his heirs male for ever - evidence of Tycho's wishes and of an expected royal visit, but never engrossed or signed.

10 January 1596 – 20 January 1596 A
familycourt & patronage
To clear his name where Gellius now resided, Tycho travelled to Lund in January 1596 accompanied by Peter Frandsen, spoke with officials of the cathedral chapter, and put five written questions to Gellius at hearings before the chapter on 10 and 20 January 1596; Gellius promised answers within six weeks. The meteorological journal's note that Tycho was 'gone to Helsingborg and Skane for ten days in January' evidently covers this circuit via Helsingborg. Immediately after the second hearing he wrote to Jorgen and Holger Rosenkrantz to shield the proceedings from court interference; on 5 February a royal missive ordered the Lund chapter to sit as a marriage court in the case.

c. August 1590 B
social visitfamilyalchemy & medicine
During Rothmann's month-long visit of August 1590, Tycho took him into Skane together with the aristocratic botanist Lauge Urne to Eriksholm Castle, where his sister Sophie Brahe lived; Rothmann admired her garden surrounding the 'distilling house' in which she prepared Paracelsian elixirs, perfumes, cosmetics and hermetically sealed preserves, and spoke of her after his return to Kassel. Zealand & the Sound

Vordingborg castle-manor B 2 documented stays
Vordingborg Castle, Zealand, Denmark · period names: Vordingborg · 55.0080, 11.9100
Medieval stronghold on Zealand's south coast, Jørgen Brahe's command 1552-57; a station of Tycho's foster childhood and presumed schooling.
1552 – 1557 (bounds uncertain) B
familyeducation
Jørgen Brahe received command of the immense medieval royal stronghold of Vordingborg on the south coast of Zealand in 1552, and Tycho passed part of his boyhood in the sprawling castle — Christianson recalls the connection when the 1597 exile caravan passed through the town. Vordingborg sat on the main route between Copenhagen and the continent: Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg came with his court in 1556, Christian III's peripatetic court stayed periodically, and Brahe, Oxe and Rud kin visited regularly — the boy's first exposure to high court traffic. The school question stays open: his autobiography has him at Latin school 'in his seventh year', and the Nationalmuseet education essay presumes ('formodentlig') Vordingborg Latin school because Jørgen was then lensmand there, but Facts of Life (1970) is silent on schooling before 1559, Dreyer and Friis have a private tutor at Tostrup instead, and Norlind doubts a formal school altogether. No school is asserted.

Held as C-grade conjecture inside a B-grade residence.

Copenhagen city A 32 documented stays
Copenhagen, Denmark · period names: Hafnia, Haffniæ, Kiøbenhavn, Kiøpnehafn · 55.6761, 12.5683
Royal capital and university city; Tycho's 1574 lectures, recurrent destination of his documented absences from Hven 1590-97, and his own Farvergade complex with the lent rampart bastion (residence there documented only for spring 1597).
19 April 1559 – 14 February 1562cal. A
educationobservationbooks & printing
Tycho arrived at the University of Copenhagen on 19 April 1559, aged twelve — the first of his family to begin university studies — under Jørgen Brahe's plan for a career in law and statecraft, lodging in the household of a professor (unnamed in Christianson 2020; Thoren suggests possibly Niels Hemmingsen). He worked through the Melanchthonian trivium while turning himself, from 1560, into an astronomer by purchase: Sacrobosco's De sphaera (used in Scavenius's lectures), the Basel 1551 Ptolemy folio bought the last day of November 1560 for two Joachimsthaler (signed and annotated, now Prague University Library, also bearing Johannes Pratensis's name), Apian's Cosmographia and Regiomontanus's De triangulis signed 'Tycho Brahe, Anno 1561' — the first appearance of the Latinised name — and the ephemerides of Carelli (bought with Jens Nilsson) and Stadius, compared for Ptolemaic against Copernican predictions. The tradition that the predicted partial solar eclipse of 21 August 1560 awakened his vocation begins with Gassendi; Norlind rejects it as aetiological myth. He left for Leipzig on 14 February 1562.

c. May 1565 – June 1565 B
in transitfamily
Landing at Copenhagen from Rostock in late May or early June 1565, Tycho learned that his foster father Jørgen Brahe — captor of the Swedish flagship in 1564 — was now vice-admiral of the fleet, deep in preparations for the next engagement. From the capital he proceeded home through Scania. Weeks later Jørgen fell into the water at the bridge between Copenhagen castle and the town while rescuing King Frederick II, and died on 21 June 1565 of the illness contracted; no source places Tycho at the deathbed or funeral, and Dreyer expressly declines to say where he resided in the following months. Norlind's pole-height list supplies independent, if inferential, support for the passage through the capital.

1572 C
books & printing
In 1572, per Christianson, Tycho took his Latin ode to his stillborn twin to the printer Mads Vingaard in Copenhagen and had it printed as his first publication - the broadsheet Carmen that antedates De nova stella by a year. The visit ties him bodily to the capital's printing trade at the very start of his publishing career, a decade before his own press on Hven. The printing itself is bibliographically certain (Nielsen 424); Tycho's personal presence at the press rests on Christianson's formulation alone.

20 July 1572 – 21 July 1572 C
court & patronagesocial visit
For King Frederick II's marriage to Sophie of Mecklenburg, held 20 July 1572 in Copenhagen Castle, the whole Danish nobility was summoned in new court attire; the next day the young queen rode to her coronation at Our Lady's, Peder Oxe carrying her crown, amid banquets, tourneys and university festivities. Thoren states Tycho 'probably borrowed attendants for the occasion and went too'; Christianson has him enrolled as a noble courtier during the wedding week, which implies presence. A probable rather than sighted attendance, at the festivity that bound him formally to the court whose patronage would shortly transform his life.

c. 1573 B
social visitbooks & printing
Early in 1573 Tycho came to Copenhagen with the manuscript of his Diarium and account of the new star, lodging as was his custom with Johannes Pratensis, professor of medicine. Pratensis had not yet heard of the star; the French envoy Charles de Dancay, dining them, thought Tycho was mocking Danish savants until a clear evening let him point the star out in the sky. Pratensis urged printing; Tycho demurred - partly the little work's want of polish, mainly the prejudice that authorship ill became a nobleman - and returned to Scania with his manuscript. The visit sat within a periodic Copenhagen pattern of these years, his circle led by Pratensis and the long-serving envoy Dancay, more than thirty years his senior. To the same pattern belongs Pratensis's surviving invitation to his Martinmas feast of 11 November 1573 — coincidentally the first anniversary of the nova discovery — though Tycho's attendance is nowhere documented.

c. 1573 B
books & printingsocial visitinstruments
During a second visit in spring 1573, after German pamphlets full of nonsense about the star had reached him, Tycho was pressed to publish not only by Pratensis but by his kinsman Peter Oxe, high treasurer of Denmark, who even suggested hiding his name in an anagram. He yielded - his consent must have preceded 16 April 1573, when Pratensis reported the figures being cut - and De nova stella was elegantly printed by Lorentz Benedicht, appearing early in the summer with the star still visible; the publication details kept him occupied past the normal spring departure times and postponed his planned journey abroad by a year. To the same Copenhagen orbit of 1573 belong the commissions to the royal clockmaker Steffen Brenner for the gilt-brass quadrant and a clockwork celestial globe.

24 April 1574 – March 1575 (bounds uncertain)cal. A
educationcourt & patronagefamilyobservation
Tycho observed at Copenhagen on 24 April 1574 and spent most of the rest of the year in the city, where his daughter Magdalene was born (day and month unrecorded) and where he kept a large town house, probably with Kirsten. Urged by Pratensis and Dancay and decided by King Frederik's own request, he opened his university lectures on 23 September 1574 with the oration on the mathematical sciences - delivered before Dancay and virtually the whole university community, defending a reformed astrology and reaching public accommodation with Niels Hemmingsen - then lectured four mornings a week on planetary theory, treating Copernicus's models in geostatic form: among the first university lectures on Copernican astronomy anywhere, and he the only nobleman of his era to teach at Copenhagen. The student Peter Jacobsen Flemlose entered his service. The lectures closed around the turn of 1574-75; before departing he wrote the Latin rag-poem asking Danish women for linen so Vedel's Saxo could be printed on Scanian paper, and left as a grand seigneur about March 1575.

1576 – 1597 (bounds uncertain) B
propertysocial visitbooks & printing
Throughout the Hven years Tycho went frequently to Copenhagen, as the Meteorological Diary shows, though nothing is known of his domestic arrangements there and no observations were made in the city. He owned a house in Farvergade in the south-west of the town; on 13 March 1589 the young king's government ordered the burgomasters to lend him the adjoining stone tower on the rampart for astronomical use (revocable if needed for defence), and on 25 March 1589 he received two empty houses next his own on condition of housing the displaced dyer. Dreyer counts the very frequent trips to Copenhagen and Scania among the burdens of the island residence, especially in winter. This recurring record anchors the diary-attested habit; individually documented Copenhagen trips stand as their own stays.

February 1576 A
social visitcourt & patronage
From Herrevad Tycho went on to Copenhagen and talked the king's offer over with his best friend Johannes Pratensis and the French envoy Charles de Dancay - the two learned friends who had long urged him toward astronomy and who would donate the Uraniborg cornerstone. He privately told Dancey, himself an emigre after decades as ambassador, of the plan to leave Denmark, and inquired into Pratensis's failing health; Pratensis divined his inclinations and wrote at the end of January assuring him his interests were respected in Denmark. Only after this consultation, and further discussion with Kirsten, his mother and his brother Steen, did he decide to accept.

18 August 1588 – 23 August 1588 A

Four months after Frederick II's death, Tycho sailed to Copenhagen on Sunday 18 August 1588 and stayed several days, speaking with the regents and mobilising his allies to secure Uraniborg's future under the new government. The lobbying - begun with visits by Kaas, Rosenkrantz and Vedel to Hven in July - bore fruit at once: on 23 August 1588 the Regency Council issued a patent proclaiming its desire to perpetuate the work of the Hven observatory, the crown having already agreed on 12 July to pay 6,000 dalers toward his building debt.

Tycho was in Copenhagen for almost two weeks, 6-18 November 1594, negotiating the terms and date of Magdalene's wedding to Gellius Sascerides. After continued negotiation through Gellius's spokesman Mogens Dallin, 15 December 1594 was fixed for the betrothal-or-wedding (the parties themselves seemed confused between the two); Gellius called on Tycho the next day, thanked him, and promised to act toward him as a son should. Tycho returned to Hven on 18 November believing the negotiations concluded.

30 November 1594 – 4 December 1594cal. A
familysocial visit
When Gellius raised new demands, Tycho sailed back into Copenhagen on 30 November 1594, presumably to attend to the wedding details, and conferred with his sister Sophie Brahe. On the evening of Tuesday 3 December he sent Niels Krag and Mogens Dallin to Gellius, who gave no clear answer; enraged, Tycho had a full summary of events drawn up and signed by Dallin, Krag, Else Mule, Sophie and himself. Next morning he stopped at Niels Krag's home to collect two Latin wedding verses of his own composing, stayed to dinner, declared he would leave public accusation to the Good Lord, and after dinner returned with Sophie to Hven - the diary noting on 4 December 'Rediit T. B. cum sorore S. B.' - to break the sad news to Magdalene. His formal declaration cancelling the wedding contract followed on 12 December.

January 1595 – 21 January 1595 A
familycourt & patronage
In January 1595 Tycho was back in Copenhagen, where he first heard of the exchange between his friends and Gellius at Venusin's house a month earlier - gossip he judged to stem from Gellius's bragging around the city - and resolved to set the record straight. Rather than trying his complaint in Consistory, the university authorities mediated a settlement: a new contract dated Copenhagen 16 January 1595, signed by Rector Nicolaus Theophilus, Bishop Peter Winstrup and professors Anders Krag, Niels Krag and Anders Christensen, by which Gellius promised not to disturb Tycho or his family. Before leaving town Tycho had Anders Krag write up his account of the December scene; he returned to Hven on 21 January to bring the news to Magdalene and her mother.

21 February 1596 – March 1596cal. A
familycourt & patronageother
On 21 February 1596 Tycho sailed to Copenhagen and was gone from Hven for a month, pursuing his case against Gellius before the university court of Consistory. On the morning after Ash Wednesday, 25 February 1596, the appellate hearings opened in the medieval Consistory building; Tycho, accompanied by Dallin, Venusin and Carl Bryske, governor of Copenhagen Castle, declared he wanted no judgment, only a notarised public record, submitted the 16 January 1595 contract, and read into evidence a list of ten false rumours, standing to declare their authors liars. On 26 February Gellius pleaded illness and sent his brother David with power of attorney. The contemporary acts printed in Danske Magazin (1746) record these sessions and further proceedings in the Convent House; on 14 April 1596 the consistorium ruled on Tycho's preface, by which time some communications went by sent notes rather than appearance.

June 1596 B
court & patronagefamily
In June 1596 Tycho was gone from Hven for nearly two weeks to attend the annual Diet of the nobility, which met to prepare the August coronation that would end the Regency. The great gathering assembled his brothers and kin at the peak of their oligarchic power: Steen Brahe on the Regency Council, Axel Brahe and Oluf Rosensparre admitted to the State Council that year, Jorgen and Knud Brahe holding the Varberg and Aarhus fiefs, cousin Steen Maltesen Sehested commanding Kronborg. His case against Gellius, however, was not ready in time for the Diet.

28 August 1596 – 9 September 1596 A
court & patronagesocial visit
Tycho left Hven from 28 August to 9 September 1596 to attend the coronation of Christian IV on 29 August, going with several famuli and wearing his golden chains with the Order of the Elephant and portrait medallions of two kings. His brother, Regent Steen Brahe, bore the royal orb; all four brothers played their parts and competed in the festive jousts while Tycho networked among the guests, including the Brandenburg court astronomer Johann Muller, who made a side-trip to Hven the day after Tycho's return, and the Scots ambassador Robert Anstruther, who also came on to Uraniborg. Bishop Peter Winstrup's sermon asserted that 'kings are gods' against the elective symbolism of the councillors' hands on the crown. It was Tycho's last great court occasion in Denmark: within a month the recall of Nordfjord, at a thousand dalers his greatest single revenue, opened the unravelling that ended in exile.

11 April 1597 – 2 June 1597cal. A
exileobservationbooks & printingalchemy & medicinepropertycourt & patronage
On Monday 11 April 1597 Tycho, Kirsten and the familia moved into the 'novum Museum Hafniense' — his own three-lot complex at the corner of Farvergade and Vestervold — with instruments on the rampart bastion granted him in 1589, the printing press and chemical laboratory in the house. The persecution peaked here: the pension had been stopped 18 March, and the assistants had already catalogued his books on Hven on 21 March; pastor Wensøsil, convicted at Roskilde 22 April, emerged from a month's dungeon to his shelter; the Hven peasants' charges were heard before the king; and in late May the town constable, on Lord Steward Walkendorf's orders, forbade him the bastion and city walls as an observatory. On 1 June he dismissed Longomontanus with a testimonial; on Thursday 2 June 1597 he left Copenhagen with a household of about twenty and every portable possession — instruments, laboratory, presses, books and papers — and never again set foot on Danish soil.

The sources disagree. Departure: Tycho's own statement 2 June 1597 (Acta 124; Christianson, Thoren, Norlind, Jonsson) vs Dreyer's inference 'between the 1st and 10th June' — 2 June followed. Start: household into Farvergade 11 April (diary; Christianson) vs Dreyer's April arrival and Thoren's rolling February–March move — 11 April taken as the residence anchor, earlier presence noted. The bastion observation ban rests solely on Tycho's own German justification (Acta 138) and 'sounds very apocryphal' (Norlind p.255), though Christianson, Dreyer and Friis report it as fact; Björklund reads the Farvergade mob riot as camarilla-staged. Gassendi's hostile-commission and break-in details are Gassendi-only (grade C colour). The book cataloguing ('Registeret vi alle junkers bøger') stands under 21 March 1597 in the diary — on Hven, before the 11 April move; Christianson's weekday 'Saturday' for the 2 June departure is a slip (Thursday, Julian).
Sorø Abbey abbey-church B 2 documented stays
Sorø Abbey, Zealand, Denmark · period names: Sora, Sorø · 55.4314, 11.5541
Secularized Cistercian abbey used by the court; Frederick II's court in residence for the Christmas season 1575, with Tycho at the table of Abbot Iver Bertelsen.
20 December 1574 C
court & patronage
On 20 December 1574 Tycho and his brothers Steen and Axel presented themselves to King Frederick II at Soro Abbey and took their leave of the court - the brothers to marry in 1575, Tycho to abandon the Copenhagen classroom and travel abroad, carrying a royal commission to scout artists, artisans and technicians for the Kronborg project. A single-source datum, exactly dated by Christianson.

The sources disagree. Single source (Christianson 2020); the artisan-scouting commission is Christianson's framing of the leave-taking.
December 1575 A
court & patronage
Back from the continental tour toward the end of 1575, Tycho presented himself to Frederick II at Soro Abbey, where the court had come for the Yuletide. He reported his recruiting mission - glassmakers, papermakers, painters, sculptors and hydraulic engineers from Hesse-Kassel, Augsburg, Nuremberg and Venice, recommending Gemperle, Schardt and Labenwolf for the Kronborg project - and told of the courts he had visited and the Regensburg coronation, supping with the king at Abbot Iver Bertelsen's table. The king, primed by the returning Danish embassy carrying Landgrave Wilhelm's strong recommendation, received him with exceptional graciousness and asked him to name his requirements in fiefs and honours - Hammershus, Visborg, Helsingborg and Landskrona were the class of option. Tycho, privately set on Basel, demurred and was told to think it over; he afterwards wrote frankly to Pratensis refusing the 'golden shackles' of castle-holding.

Ven (Hven) island A 2 documented stays
Ven (Hven) island, Landskrona municipality, Sweden · period names: Hven, Hveen, Huenna, Hvenna · 55.9060, 12.6945
Island in the Øresund, Danish until 1658; Tycho's lifetime fief 1576-97 and the seat of Uraniborg, Stjerneborg, the printing house and the paper mill (all carried as separate sites, not places). He never returned after 1597 (nv-hven-after-1597).
Hven (Ven) — the island fief extant A 1576–1597
The island of Hven (Swedish Ven) in the Øresund, granted to Tycho as a fief by Frederik II on 23 May 1576 - rent-free for as long as he lived and continued his mathematical studies, with 400 daler from the treasury toward a house he was to build on the island (Tycho himself supplying the stone and lime; Kancelliets Brevbøger 1576-79 p.59). Uraniborg — the castle of the heavens ruined A 1576–1580
Tycho's great house, built 1576–1580 on a square rampart-enclosed plot whose four corners pointed to the compass points, with four roads running from those corners to the raised circular space at the centre where the house stood. The central building was a square 49 feet on a side, with round towers 18 feet in diameter on its north and south faces (ringed by lower outhouses for fuel) and narrow en… full record in Tabula →
The gardens and ramparts of Uraniborg reconstructed B 1576; redesigned after 1590
The square earthwork ramparts enclosing Uraniborg, their corners set to the cardinal points, with formal gardens and orchards within and around them — among the finest in Scandinavia by Tycho's own account. Christianson describes the orchard's pippin, Rambour and Gylling apples, Doyenné and blood pears, green and blue Reine Claude plums, morello cherries, apricots, figs, quince and walnuts, and kn… full record in Tabula →
The alchemical laboratory lost B 1580
The alchemical laboratory in Uraniborg's basement, fitted with sixteen furnaces of nine different kinds — Tycho's 'terrestrial astronomy', where he prepared medicines (the celebrated plague elixirs) and pursued the Paracelsian correspondence of macrocosm and microcosm. Visitors were taken down to see it, alchemy having at least as much lay appeal as astronomy; at the basement's other end lay cella… full record in Tabula →
The library and the great globe lost B 1580
Uraniborg's library, which among its treasures held the great brass globe (globus magnus orichalcicus) onto which Tycho engraved his measured star positions. The library was the documentary heart of the establishment, feeding the press and the observing programme. full record in Tabula →
Stjerneborg — the star castle reconstructed A 1584
A separate, largely subterranean observatory built in 1584 just south of Uraniborg: five crypts beneath rotating cupolas, each giving one of the largest instruments a permanent, wind-sheltered mounting on solid ground. Stjerneborg ('star castle') answered the chief defect of Uraniborg's high galleries — that wind and an unstable footing spoiled the finest measurements. The printing house (Tycho's press) lost A 1584
Tycho's own printing house, established on Hven in 1584 so that he controlled his own means of publication and distribution. Its earliest known imprint is the memorial broadsheet Epitaphium Johannis Pratensis (1584); the earliest DATED piece is the occasional poem Carmen ad Jacobum Ulfeldium, inscribed 'Uraniburgi, 7 Kal. The paper mill lost B 1589–1597
The paper mill on Hven that fed Tycho's press — its production a recurring concern in the correspondence (the two papermakers who absconded delayed the Progymnasmata, as Tycho complained to Hájek). Tycho Brahe Museum & the Stjerneborg reconstruction extant A 20th–21st c.
The modern Tycho Brahe Museum on Ven, centred on the excavated and reconstructed crypts of Stjerneborg and the foundations of Uraniborg, with a recreated Renaissance garden — the principal place where Tycho's establishment can be seen today. full record in Tabula →
1576 – 29 March 1597 (bounds uncertain)cal. A
observationinstrumentsbooks & printingalchemy & medicinecourt & patronagepropertyfamily
The two-decade anchor residence. Frederik II's forleningsbrev of 23 May 1576 granted Hven rent-free for life so long as he pursued his mathematical studies, with 400 daler toward a house; Dancay laid Uraniborg's foundation stone at sunrise on 8 August 1576, and the solar series begun on Tycho's thirtieth birthday, 14 December 1576, opened an unbroken observational run to 15 March 1597. He commuted from the mainland until autumn 1576; Kirsten and the children settled from late 1577, the household moving into Uraniborg in November 1580. Around it grew Stjerneborg (from 1584), the sixteen-furnace laboratory, the instrument workshop, the printing office (1584) and paper mill (1592), and a familia of up to a dozen assistants; De mundi (1588) and the Epistolae astronomicae (1596) issued from the island press, and the comet of 13 November 1577 was sighted from his fishponds. Royal visitors included Queen Sophie (1586), James VI of Scotland (20 March 1590) and the king-elect Christian (3 July 1592, the gilt globe exchanged for the king's portrait on a gold chain). Dated Uraniborg autographs pin bodily presence across 1586-1596. Every documented off-island trip is itemised as its own stay.

The sources disagree. Foundation-stone date: Tycho's Mechanica gives 8 August 1576, the Lund fragment reads 1 August; Norlind supports 8 August astronomically (moon in Aquarius) - 8 August adopted. Departure date: 29 March 1597 (Thoren from Tycho's own statement; Dreyer's conclusion against the ledger's impossible '29 Aprilis'; Jonsson 'probably') vs 11 April (Christianson, diary entry of the household entering the Copenhagen museum) vs 29 April (Nielsen) - 29 March adopted for the end of residence, final resolution left to the period-7 reconciliation. Gassendi's index dates Christian's royal visit 1591; all modern sources 3 July 1592 - 1592 followed. Norlind (after Yrwing 1955) reads the departure as a feint to force restoration of income, which Thoren registers and finds unconvincing. Bjorklund's Bilag 4 dates the prebend loss 1596; Christianson/Thoren document the Roskilde canonry's transfer to Friis on 10 June 1597. First Hven solar observation: 14 December 1576 (Dreyer, Thoren, Jönsson) vs 13 December (Christianson 2020 p. 85) — 14 December adopted.
22 February 1576 A
observationpropertyin transit
Four days after the Frederiksborg audience Tycho crossed to the island in the Oresund to acquaint himself with his new workplace - his first known visit, as its incoming lord over Tuna's freeholding peasants - and the same evening took his first observation there, a close conjunction of Mars and the moon ('Observatio haec facta in Huenna'). The formal fee of the island followed by royal letter given at Frederiksborg on 23 May 1576, the same day the treasurer Walkendorff was ordered to pay 400 daler toward building a house on Hven - the first documentary trace of Uraniborg.

Ibstrup court A 1 documented stay
Ibstrup hunting lodge (later Jægersborg), Gentofte, Denmark · period names: Ibstrup, jaktslottet Ibstrup · 55.7700, 12.5700
Royal hunting lodge north of Copenhagen; scene of Frederick II's offer of Hven to Tycho on 11 February 1576. Thoren's unnamed 'king's hunting lodge' (frederiks-hunting-lodge cluster) is folded in here.
Long demolished; Bernstorff palace stands close to the site (Dreyer).
11 February 1576 A
court & patronage
Obeying the pre-dawn summons, Tycho rode from Knutstorp the same day and reached the royal hunting lodge of Ibstrup (later Jaegersborg) north of Copenhagen before sunset. The chamberlain Niels Parsberg - brother of his Rostock duelling opponent - showed him into the royal chamber, where in a long private audience Frederick II, who knew of the Basel emigration plan and had lately viewed Hven from the rising Kronborg, offered him the island for his experiments in astronomy and distillation, promising buildings and income so that foreigners would come to Denmark to see and learn. Tycho noted the island's dangerous landings, promised serious consideration, and was told to bring his answer to Frederiksborg. His own account, written three days later, is the primary source.
PeopleFrederick IIking, made the Hven offer in private audienceNiels Parsbergcourt chamberlain, usher; brother of Manderup Parsberg

Frederiksborg castle-manor B 1 documented stay
Frederiksborg Castle, Hillerød, Denmark · period names: Frederiksborg · 55.9350, 12.3011
Frederick II's principal hunting-castle residence in north Zealand.
18 February 1576 A
court & patronage
One week after the Ibstrup audience, having consulted Pratensis and Dancay and certainly his mother, brother and Steen Bille, Tycho rode on 18 February 1576 to Frederiksborg Castle and accepted his sovereign's offer, renewing his service to Frederick II on new terms: an immediate annual pension of 500 dalers - nearly doubling his income - against his promise to be loyal and ready to serve when summoned. This audience formalised the contract of service that framed the whole Hven enterprise; the formal grant of the island followed on 23 May 1576, quit and free, with 400 dalers toward a residence.

Sound-toll town opposite Hven; Kronborg was Frederick II's new fortress whose craftsmen milieu also served Uraniborg. Bodily presence at the castle itself is disputed — the danish-context package finds no documented visit (nv-kronborg).
1 July 1577 B
court & patronage
On 1 July 1577 Tycho delivered at Kronborg the extensive horoscope for the crown prince Christian, born 12 April 1577 - written in Latin with a summarising German section for Queen Sophie. It predicted a problem-free childhood, survival of a grave illness at about twelve, a life of 56-57 years under God's reservation, and a character fond of hunting and war; Tycho stressed that a four-minute error of the castle clock at the birth could overturn the whole prognosis. The astrologer-royal-adviser role in full function, five kilometres across the Sound from his building site.

The sources disagree. Only Jonsson names Kronborg as the delivery place; Dreyer dates the delivery of the horoscope 1 July 1577 without naming where. Kronborg kept at grade B on the location.
c. 1578 C
court & patronagesocial visit
On a visit to Kronborg around 1578 Tycho met the master mason Hans van Steenwinckel, experienced in architectural design with a knack for perspective drawing; he invited him to Hven, taught him geometry, astronomy and Vitruvian architectural theory, and made him the practical builder of Uraniborg's complex roofs and later designer of Stjerneborg and the Hven mill house. Kronborg was the court pole of Tycho's world - artisans like Schardt and Labenwolf worked at both castle and villa - and such visits doubtless recurred, though this is the only one Christianson individually attests.

30 June 1592 A
court & patronagein transit
Plague on Hven had forced postponement of the king-elect's intended visit (Tycho sent his pupil Cort Axelsen across on 30 April 1592 to warn him off at the shore). When the disease vanished, Tycho himself crossed to Zealand on 30 June 1592 to the manor of Horsholm, where the fifteen-year-old prince was residing against the plague, to announce that the visit could proceed; the governor could find no excuse to prevent it. Christian came to Hven on 3 July with three councillors, exchanged gifts - the self-moving gilt brass globe against a gold chain with his portrait - and promised support for training young men in navigation and astronomy. The 3 July visit is on Hven and belongs to the anchor stay.

Cathedral city; seat of Tycho's prebend of the Chapel of the Three Holy Kings from 1579. The chancery sweep never documents him bodily in Roskilde — chapel business ran by letter and bailiff (nv-roskilde-prebend); the stays rest on the biographical sources.
26 September 1594 A
property
Stung by a sharp royal reprimand over the ruinous state of the Chapel of the Three Holy Kings - with the threat that the canonry fief would be regranted if repairs were not done by Christmas - Tycho went to Roskilde on 26 September 1594 with Hans van Steenwinckel (or another master builder), inspected the chapel, and worked out a plan to replace the vaults with a flat beamed ceiling. The one documented bodily visit in a prebend tenure otherwise conducted entirely by letter.
PeopleHans van Steenwinckelmaster builder, joint inspector of the chapel
