The sources disagree. The crown-fiefs KB sweep found all chapel business conducted by letter and no chancery entry placing Tycho in Roskilde (the vault-removal permission is 8 Nov 1594); Christianson's dated inspection stands as the exception, not a contradiction. Thoren's separate suggestion that Tycho 'may have been at Roskilde checking the work on the chapel roof' in November 1594 is his own hedge and is not promoted to a stay.
17 April 1597 – 20 April 1597cal. A
othersocial visitin transit
Tycho travelled to Roskilde on Sunday 17 April 1597 — the meteorological diary records 'Profectus est Tycho Roschyldiam' — into a stormy night and next-day blizzard, in the week of the church-ordinance prosecution of his Hven pastor Jens Jensen Wensøsil, tried before Bishop Peter Winstrup on Friday 22 April with the Kronborg commander Ditlev Holck sent to 'assist'. On Wednesday 20 April he met his brothers Steen and Axel Brahe, both state councillors, presumably concerting a defence. Wensøsil was convicted on both charges — omitting exorcism, and failing to punish Tycho, 'who for eighteen years has not taken Holy Eucharist but has lived an evil life with a mistress'. The real target was Tycho himself; he still held the prebend of the Holy Three Kings chapel there, lost on 10 June to the chancellor. The diary stops abruptly on 22 April 1597, never resumed.

Queen Mother Sophie had invested Jørgen Brahe with the fief and command of Nykøbing in 1555, and in 1557, having relinquished his royal fief in the power struggle that preceded Peder Oxe's fall, Jørgen transferred his seat to the island fortress between Lolland and Falster. On Thoren's 'presumably followed' reading of the foster household, the ten-to-twelve-year-old Tycho lived there until he was sent to Copenhagen in April 1559. Christianson notes that Jørgen also commanded Nykøbing but attaches Tycho's boyhood residence only to Vordingborg; the stay is therefore single-source and inferential.

Like the other Danish road stations of June 1597, this is Christianson's reconstruction of the standard southern route rather than an independently documented halt; Tycho's presence on the road between Copenhagen (2 June) and Rostock (mid-June) is itself secure.

Denmark (place unspecified), Denmark · period names: patria
Region-blob cluster holding imprecisely-located stays ('in patria', presence in Denmark between journeys) where Gassendi and Joensson name no residence.
c. June 1567 – December 1567 B
familypropertysocial visit
Home from Rostock for the second half of 1567, scarred and wearing the prosthesis, in a country strained by the Seven Years' War: the Scanian borderlands lay wasted and his father Otte — promoted in 1567 to the front-line governorship of Helsingborg Castle — was organising a fresh offensive. Tycho ordered his affairs, visited kinsmen and friends ('better than I deserved', he later wrote of his reception), and announced against the expectations of his class that he would continue his scientific studies; Otte was among those upset, while Steen Bille, Peder Oxe, Inger Oxe and Beate Bille showed understanding. Christianson infers that the Christmas-holiday discussions with Peder Oxe and Steen Bille moved them to broker the Roskilde canonry charter that followed in spring 1568. He stayed through his twenty-first birthday and the holidays, then embarked on the third journey. No source names the residence; Thoren has him 'surely' with the family in their new Helsingborg quarters.

Tycho went off to Jutland for the wedding of his brother Knud Brahe to Margaret Lange, celebrated at Bygholm Castle on 23 August 1584 and hosted by the bride's brother Erik Lange of Bygholm, the gold-making alchemist. He had sent his new Equatorial Armillary back for adjustments on 20 August before departing. The connection made here mattered: Lange's visit to Uraniborg followed a month later with his 'boy' Nicolaus Reymers in tow, seeding both the Ursus plagiarism feud and, through Sophie Brahe's later betrothal to Lange, the Urania Titani poem.

The embarkation point is Christianson's reconstruction; other sources have the ship taken at Copenhagen itself (Gassendi, Jonsson) or the route run via Lübeck (Norlind).

German lands

Wittenberg university A 7 documented stays
Lutherstadt Wittenberg, Germany · period names: Witeberga, Witteberga, Vitebergae · 51.8662, 12.6471
Electoral Saxon university town: the five-month stay of 1566 (without matriculation) and the 236-day plague-refuge sojourn of October 1598 - 14 June 1599, lodging in Melanchthon's former house, then occupied by Johannes Jessenius. The claimed 1568 pass-through is a phantom (nv-wittenberg-1568).
February 1562 – March 1562 B
in transit
A waypoint of the outward journey, not yet a study station. Having crossed the southern Baltic in February 1562, Tycho and Vedel travelled up the Elbe to Wittenberg and continued overland — Thoren has them riding two more days — to Leipzig, where both were registered on 24 March 1562. Tycho's Wittenberg study residence belongs to a later period.

May 1565 B
in transitsocial visit
First touch of Wittenberg, in transit on the homeward road from Leipzig in May 1565. Thoren has Tycho and Vedel pass through purposefully, to see his former instructor Bartholomew Schultz (Scultetus), who had moved there the previous autumn; Friis conjectures a call on Caspar Peucer; Gassendi records only a regretted transit (in transcursu), the regret that motivated the deliberate residence of 1566. Norlind grounds the passage independently in the pole-height list of the oldest observation journal, whose sequence Leipzig–Wittenberg–Rostock he reads as the route home, and notes that Stephanius's later phrase 'rediit Wittebergam' for 1566 presupposes this earlier visit.

15 April 1566 – 16 September 1566cal. A
education
The second study journey's first station: Tycho arrived at Wittenberg on 15 April 1566, this time with the M.A. Hans Aalborg as preceptor rather than a noble hovmester, finding Vedel already there completing his degree among the traditional Danish student colony. The leading connection was Caspar Peucer, Melanchthon's son-in-law, professor of medicine and Preceptor primarius, whose teaching Tycho attended for a time — though he never formally matriculated (a lack he remedied ceremonially only in February 1599) and lodged with no professor, perhaps with Schultz. After five months plague broke out in the congested town and caused a general student exodus: he left on 16 September 1566 and reached Rostock on the 24th, an eight-day journey.

9 September 1570 A
in transit
The one fixed point on the previously unknown homeward route from Augsburg: an album amicorum leaf of the Frenchman Claudius Textor (matriculated Wittenberg 1564), now in the Germanisches Nationalmuseum, Nuremberg, carries Tycho's autograph verses — six lines on the stars inclining but not compelling the rational soul — signed 'Witteberge: Anno: 1570: sept: 9.' It is the oldest known Tycho album autograph, and Norlind's discovery of it proved Tycho was in Wittenberg on 9 September 1570, certainly on the journey home to Denmark, nearly four months after his last Augsburg observation. The unhurried pace tells against the tradition that his father's illness triggered the departure.

c. November 1575 – December 1575 B
in transitinstrumentssocial visit
The last recorded station of the tour. At Wittenberg Tycho sought out Wolfgang Schuler, who had observed the new star with a parallax of nineteen minutes, expressly to inspect the instruments behind the figure: the large wooden triquetrum (probably built by Johannes Praetorius), still locally regarded as a great achievement, which Tycho found by no means as excellent as reported - marvelling that respected astronomers could think such a mean instrument sufficient - and the wooden quadrant with which the elder Reinhold had fixed the Wittenberg pole altitude, whose value Tycho judged nearly a sixth of a degree too great. He also found the university in chaos from the Elector's crypto-Calvinist purge, Caspar Peucer imprisoned, before completing the journey home to Denmark by the year's end.

25 October 1598 A
in transit
A dated album leaf — 'Suspiciendo despicio', Tycho's personal device (Sotheby's Paris, 15 December 2004, lot 36) — places him bodily at Wittenberg on 25 October 1598, between the Magdeburg week and the Dresden month. The Elbe road from Magdeburg to Dresden passed through Wittenberg, where, per Thoren, the Jessenius acquaintance was first made in passing; the leaf is therefore read as a transit attestation on the outward leg, not the start of the winter residence, which the biographies date from 4 December. A candidate host album, Johann Nesen's Stammbuch (Zittau, Christian-Weise-Bibliothek B 178, the Tycho leaf excised), records the entry under 26 October 1598 — a one-day discrepancy unresolved. An undated 1598 Wittenberg entry now trimmed into the Merseburg autograph collection belongs either to this passage or to the December residence.

4 December 1598 – 14 June 1599cal. A
exileeducationbooks & printingobservationalchemy & medicinesocial visit
Tycho and his sons arrived in Wittenberg on 4 December 1598 and lodged with the anatomist Johannes Jessenius (Jan Jesenský) in Philipp Melanchthon's former house — later Caspar Peucer's, known to Tycho from his 1566 student days. He set up a chemical laboratory on the ground floor, observed the sun's meridian altitude on 9 December, and gathered a circle including the mathematician Melchior Jöstelius (who perfected prosthaphaeresis with him), the theologian Ägidius Hunnius and the poet Friedrich Taubmann. The total lunar eclipse of 31 January 1599 ran nearly half an hour against his lunar theory, halting the Progymnasmata Moon-section printing for recalculation — a manuscript ephemeris for 1599 was substituted as imperial gift. In February 1599, never before formally matriculated, he enrolled with his sons and famulus Johannes Eriksen; the rector feted him at the castle. Kirsten and the daughters, from Wandsburg 6 January, arrived mid-January. Coraduz's summons matured through the spring, but carriage horses, Magdalene's grave illness, thaw and floods delayed departure until 14 June 1599 — the farewell album leaf 'quo Witebergā discessi'. The densest dated-autograph run of his life spans the stay: 14 January (Hagecius Mechanica dedication), 28 February (his son's album), 6 March (Sinnich), 16 April (the Palingenius leaf, Sophia stock 6196), 8 and 29 May.

The sources disagree. Arrival: 4 December 1598 (Christianson p.302, Norlind p.298; Dreyer 'first week of December') vs the internal stores' c.21 October back-calculation from a 236-day figure and Nielsen's 'Oct 1598' interlude start — 4 December followed, the 25 October leaf read as an en-route touch. Departure: 'at Easter 1599' (Nielsen; Dreyer and Friis 'shortly after Easter'; Gassendi 'not before Easter, for the floods') vs the dated leaves of 16 April, 8 and 29 May and the 14 June 1599 farewell self-dating (Christianson, Norlind) — 14 June governs. Length: Jessenius's funeral oration says nine months; the documented span is about six and a half; the stores' 236-day figure (implying October arrival) is unexplained. Cause of the halt: plague at Prague and the scattered court (all biographies, Gassendi, Jonsson) vs Šíma-Valeška's express rejection of the plague explanation — the plague account is far better attested but the objection is flagged. Calendar of 14 June: Thoren 'corrects Norlind' toward old style, yet Norlind's own text prints '14 juni 1599 g.st.' — an extraction-level discrepancy, both in fact Julian. Family logistics: women from Wandsburg 6 January, arrived mid-January (Christianson) vs Dreyer's 'escorted by Longomontanus as far as Magdeburg, joined during the winter' vs Friis's separate route 'via Magdeburg to Dresden'. Dreyer additionally has the post-Easter departure leave the family 'half way, at Dresden' — against Christianson's 14 June departure 'with all his familia'; the day-dated leaf governs, the Dresden family-parking belongs, if real, to the 1599 journey (p8).
Leipzig university A 1 documented stay
Leipzig, Germany · period names: Lipsia · 51.3397, 12.3731
Electoral Saxon university city of the first study tour (1562-65), nominally for law. The claimed second journey of November 1565 is a phantom (nv-leipzig-1565-second).
24 March 1562 – 17 May 1565cal. A
educationobservationinstrumentsbooks & printing
Tycho reached Leipzig on 24 March 1562, five and a half weeks out of Copenhagen, with the twenty-year-old Anders Sørensen Vedel as preceptor, and matriculated as 'Ticho Brade ex Scandia'. Sent to read law, he lodged in a professor's household and studied astronomy secretly at night: a fist-sized celestial globe hidden from Vedel, Stadius's ephemerides, then the Alphonsine and Prutenic tables. The Saturn–Jupiter conjunction of August 1563, which the tables missed badly, prompted his first observation log, headed 'Anno 1563, seventeen years of age, Leipzig'. Sightings taken first with large compasses gave way from 1 May 1564 to a cross-staff after Gemma Frisius, transversal-divided by Bartholomaeus Scultetus, for whose faulty divisions he computed a correction table. His circle included Homelius, Camerarius and the electoral mathematician Valentin Thau; he also cast nativities, Peucer's among them. He and Vedel left on 17 May 1565.

Rostock university A 5 documented stays
Rostock, Germany · period names: Rostochium · 54.0889, 12.1400
Hanseatic university city; study residence 1566-68 (the duel that cost Tycho part of his nose was fought here in December 1566) and first continental station of the 1597 exile.
25 May 1565 – May 1565cal. A
in transit
Tycho and Vedel reached Rostock on 25 May 1565, eight days after leaving Leipzig (17 May, Hegelund's date) — the Baltic port's first appearance in his itinerary, as a mere embarkation point a year before it became his residence. The Northern Seven Years' War was in full course and hostile fleets cruised the Baltic, but merchant sailings continued and the pair crossed to Copenhagen without meeting hostile cruisers. The 25 May date rests on the Stephanius notes and is reported unanimously.

24 September 1566 – 1567cal. A
educationobservationalchemy & medicine
First Rostock residence: arrived 24 September 1566, matriculated in October under rector Simon Pauli, lodging in the household of the theologian Lucas Bacmeister. No one taught astronomy, but the Paracelsian Levinus Battus and the empiricist Heinrich Brucaeus opened his lifelong medical-alchemical interests. On the lunar eclipse of 28 October 1566 he posted anonymous Latin verses foretelling Sultan Süleyman's death — the sultan had died on 9 September, before the prediction. At a betrothal dance in Bacmeister's house on 10 December he quarrelled with his kinsman Manderup Parsberg; the quarrel flared again on 27 December and on 29 December, about seven in the evening in deep darkness, a duel cost Tycho the bridge of his nose, concealed thereafter by a prosthesis. He observed the solar eclipse of 9 April 1567 at Rostock — 'the first he observed as a real astronomer' — and went home in the summer of 1567, departure undated.

The sources disagree. Cause of the quarrel — the primary note is read two ways: Norlind (p. 22) renders Stephanius 'propter choream' (over the dance), while Christianson's edition of the same note (Facts of Life 1970, p. 24) has the dispute arising 'concerning the movements of the stars' at the Bacmeister betrothal; Gassendi's specific prowess-contest version rests on a misreading of Laurus and is rejected (Norlind). The underlying cause is not settled. Duel date: 10/27/29 December 1566 sequence adopted (Stephanius, Norlind, danish-context); Gassendi notes some referred the incident to October 1565 — rejected. Venue: Christianson 2000 places the duel in Bacmeister's house; Thoren (Stolterfoht tradition) and Jönsson a churchyard by night — quarrel indoors, duel outside adopted. Prosthesis: Gassendi's wax-gold-silver and Dreyer's gold-and-silver composition are debunked — copper-zinc alloy (brass) with traces of gold per the 1901/2012 exhumations (Debunked Claims Register). Jessenius's funeral-oration version (an assassin's night attack) was formally protested: Christian IV's letter of 4 May 1602 insists the two duelled 'redlich fur der faust'.
1 January 1568 – 1568 A
educationobservationalchemy & medicinecourt & patronage
Second Rostock residence: Tycho dashed back without a tutor, arriving on New Year's Day 1568, lodging two weeks with the Paracelsian Levinus Battus before taking his own rooms in the Jurists' College — 'a very suitable place for observing' — and resuming observation on 2 January. His letter of 14 January 1568 to Hans Aalborg, the earliest preserved of his whole correspondence, asked him to 'bury in deep silence the cause of my departure' from home. The university levied a stiff fine of twenty Joachimsthalers, probably over the Parsberg duel; Brucaeus and Peder Oxe's influence aided the appeal, which proceeded without him. By royal letters patent dated Copenhagen 14 May 1568 — the first royal favour shown him, credited to Peder Oxe — he was promised the next vacant canonry at Roskilde cathedral, probably received at Rostock; law study yielded to his own formation, and he left, departure undated, for the south.

The stop is Thoren's inference alone: no document places Tycho in Rostock in 1570, and the stay is recorded at the corresponding grade.

June 1597 – 8 September 1597cal. A
exilecourt & patronagepropertysocial visit
Tycho and his familia of about twenty settled into temporary quarters in Rostock around mid-June 1597, warmly received in his old student city — Chytraeus wrote a welcoming note on 16 June, and Lucas Bacmeister still kept the house of the 1566 duel. At St Mary's he took Holy Eucharist with his family for the first time in eighteen years. On 10 July he sent Christian IV the proud Danish-language letter defending his departure and offering to continue his work 'on fair conditions'; the crushing answer, dated 8 October, reached him only at Wandsbek. He sought Duke Ulrich of Mecklenburg's intercession (late July), wrote Erik Sparre on 7 September about a Baltic island from King Sigismund, and lent the young Mecklenburg dukes 10,000 daler at 12 per cent, bond dated 24 August, secured on Amt Doberan — he had not left Denmark impoverished. Plague striking the town, he accepted Rantzau's Holstein invitation and left on 8 September 1597. Sent originals to Moritz of Hesse-Kassel (17 July) and Sparre (7 September) anchor presence.

The Moritz-of-Hesse letter is labelled 17 July 1597 but its tekstnet slug reads 15970617001 (17 June); if June is right the arrival was earlier — unresolved in the stores. Norlind corrects the frequent claim that the king's 8 October answer reached Tycho in Rostock: it found him at Wandsbek.
Freiburg im Breisgau university B 1 documented stay
Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany · period names: Freiburg, Freiburg im Breisgau · 47.9945, 7.8460
Near Basel; seat of Oswald Schreckenfuchs, visited on the Basel journey.
1568 – 1569 (bounds uncertain) B
social visitinstruments
From Basel Tycho visited Erasmus Oswald Schreckenfuchs, professor of mathematics at nearby Freiburg im Breisgau, admiring his collection of instruments and noting celestial models that demonstrated planetary motions according to the theories of Ptolemy and Copernicus — an early exposure to mechanical representations of the rival world systems, and one of the deliberate calls on astronomical authorities that punctuated this tour. The acquaintance bore fruit: in 1575 he would order a zodiacal armillary from Schreckenfuchs.

Travelling south from Rostock in 1568 on the tour that would end in Basel and Augsburg, Tycho stopped in Nuremberg and purchased a fine cross-staff and a set of astronomical rings made by Walter Arscenius, nephew of Gemma Frisius — his first significant instrument purchases from the great south-German artisan market. The stop is attested by Christianson 2020 alone among the swept sources and is graded accordingly.

November 1575 B
social visitinstrumentsin transit
Starting north after the coronation, Tycho stopped in Nuremberg, centre of the German clock and instrument trade. He met Joachim Camerarius the Younger, physician-son of the humanist - the friendship 'contracted in a short time' that Tycho's first letter to him of November 1576 (TBOO VII, 42) fixes to this visit - and visited the shop of the fountain-maker Georg Labenwolf, whom he recommended for the Kronborg works and who later built Uraniborg's hydraulics. The contacts made here brought Nuremberg artisans to Denmark in 1577; the sculptor Johan Gregor van der Schardt was probably first met here or at Regensburg.

c. 1569 B
in transitsocial visit
Passing through Ingolstadt on the Danube, Tycho called on Philip Apian — son of Peter Apian of Astronomicum Caesareum fame, whose Cosmography Tycho had used to teach himself astronomy — a keen observer of heavens and earth whose huge triangulated map of Bavaria, printed at his own officin, was one of the cartographic marvels of the age; Håkansson suggests the visit may seriously have awakened the cartographic interest Tycho later applied to the Øresund region. The visit's date is the most contested waypoint of the tour: Norlind shows Apian was expelled from Ingolstadt for suspected heresy only in October 1569, making a call in spring 1569, on the road from Basel to Augsburg, the likeliest reading — followed here with Thoren.

Lauingen town A 1 documented stay
Lauingen an der Donau, Germany · period names: Lauinga, Lauingen, Lauingen in Suabia · 48.5686, 10.4297
Swabian Danube town; home of Cyprianus Leovitius, visited from Augsburg.
c. 1569 A
social visitin transit
Following the Danube from Basel early in 1569 (Norlind: end of 1568 or spring 1569), Tycho called at Lauingen in Swabia on Cyprianus Leovitius, the famous astrologer of the Saturn-Jupiter conjunctions and ephemeride-maker whose tables he had used as a student. Invited home, he drew dinner out deep into the night in astronomical conversation — and made the astonished discovery that this leading astronomer-astrologer never actually observed the heavens, owning no instruments and timing eclipses only with friends' clocks. The exchange sharpened his conviction that only a sustained course of observation could yield correct planetary tables, and strengthened his resolve on his chosen path. The encounter is recorded by Tycho himself (TBOO III, 221) and reported by every biographical tradition.

Augsburg city A 2 documented stays
Augsburg, Germany · period names: Augusta Vindelicorum · 48.3705, 10.8978
Imperial free city; the Hainzel brothers' humanist circle and the instrument-making milieu (Schissler); Tycho's Quadrans Maximus stood at Paul Hainzel's Goeggingen estate outside the walls.
14 April 1569 – 16 May 1570 A
instrumentsobservationalchemy & medicinesocial visiteducation
The longest stop of the tour: some fourteen months in the imperial city, his observations there running from 14 April 1569 to 16 May 1570, with departure soon after. Admiring the city's fortifications, fountains and civic culture, he settled among its humanist patriciate — the brothers Paul and Johann Baptist Hainzel, the rector-librarian Hieronymus Wolf, the schoolman Johannes Major — and here established instrument-making as his metier: his first self-designed instrument, the great half-arc, was usable by November 1569; he designed his first sextant, left as a parting gift to Paul Hainzel; and he commissioned the great celestial globe of 1.5 m, unfinished at his departure and left in Hainzel's care. With Paul Hainzel he built the gargantuan oak Quadrans Maximus at Göggingen. Wolf introduced him to Petrus Ramus, in Augsburg in April 1570, who urged an astronomy rebuilt on observation without hypotheses. He was increasingly drawn to alchemy — the 'spagyrical arts' — from this period, and left, reluctantly and somewhat impromptu, probably in May 1570.

The sources disagree. Landlord: Christianson 2020 p. 36 names the goldsmith and Paracelsian Lorenz Thenn; Norlind pp. 25-26 a Danish countryman, magister Laurentius 'Den Danus' — plausibly the same Laurentius differently identified; both kept, neither asserted over the other. Globe maker: Thoren (following the tradition also in Jönsson and Tycho Brahes Verden) has Christoph Schissler make the 1.5 m globe core; Christianson 2020 says 'an unknown maker' and Norlind 'an Augsburg craftsman'; Mosley finds the Schissler attribution inconclusive, reading Johannes Maior's letter of 1 August 1576 (TBOO VII, 36.5-26) against it — left open, Schissler flagged as unproven. The Schissler workshop visit itself is Mosley's conjecture, not an assertion. Quadrant garden: all modern sources place it on Paul Hainzel's Göggingen estate; within Gassendi the funeral oration says Johann Baptist's garden while the index says Paul's. Departure: soon after 16 May 1570 (Thoren, Christianson 2020, Norlind) against Friis's 'toward the end of the year' — superseded by the Textor album leaf placing Tycho at Wittenberg on 9 September 1570.
c. August 1575 – October 1575 A
instrumentssocial visitin transit
In late summer 1575 Tycho and Flemlose came from Italy to Augsburg, renewing the old circle - the Hainzel brothers, Hieronymus Wolf - though the second stay proved anticlimactic: the great Goggingen quadrant had been destroyed by a windstorm in December 1574 and left unrepaired, and Schissler's long-awaited celestial globe, ordered in 1570, proved imperfectly spherical and cracked at the joints. He prepared the globe for transport - it was freighted with great difficulty to Denmark the following year, trued with parchment, clad in brass and perfected on Hven, carrying the stars of his catalogue by 1595. He recruited the portrait artist Tobias Gemperlin into his service, the future painter of the mural-quadrant portrait, and scouted artisans for Frederick II, lingering into late October before dropping downriver to the Regensburg coronation.

Göggingen observatory-site B 1 documented stay
Göggingen (district of Augsburg), Germany · period names: Goggingen, Göggingen · 48.3500, 10.8700
Paul Hainzel's country estate just outside Augsburg; site of the great oak Quadrans Maximus erected 1570 to Tycho's design.
1 April 1570 – 16 May 1570 A
observationinstruments
In the park of Paul Hainzel's country estate at Göggingen, just south-west of Augsburg, a crew of some twenty men erected the colossal oak Quadrans Maximus of Tycho's design — nearly 5.5 metres in radius (c. 14 cubits), brass scale divided to minutes and fractions of minutes, built in about a month, apparently March 1570, at Hainzel's cost. Tycho recorded his first observation with it on 1 April 1570 and observed at roughly weekly intervals; on 16 May 1570 he and Hainzel observed the Sun together with it for the last time. Petrus Ramus went out to the suburban villa after dinner to see 'a great machine he has invented' and debated whether an astronomy without hypotheses was possible. The quadrant — Tycho's first work with a large instrument, whose results he said agreed wholly with those later obtained in Denmark — stood in the open under tarpaulins, remained in use as late as 1577 by Nørlind's account; Dreyer instead has it destroyed by storm in December 1574.

Kassel court A 1 documented stay
Kassel, Germany · period names: Cassel, Cassellae, in Hassiam · 51.3127, 9.4797
Court and balcony observatory of Landgrave Wilhelm IV of Hesse-Kassel, visited at Easter 1575; Tycho never returned — the later collaboration ran by correspondence and emissaries (nv-kassel-after-1575).
March 1575 – April 1575 A
observationinstrumentscourt & patronagesocial visit
First station of the 1575 tour: Tycho arrived with Flemlose a few days before Easter (3 April 1575) at the court of Landgrave Wilhelm IV, who had observed from the Zwehrer Thor since 1561. For more than a week - Gassendi says eight or ten days - the two conversed by day and observed by night: the nova's parallax, the retardation of the sun at the horizon (the refraction problem Tycho resolved to pursue, recalling Bernhard Walther), the position of Spica, the landgrave's azimuth quadrants, great celestial clock and Baldewein globe. Gifts were exchanged - the landgrave's star catalogue for De nova stella. When the infant Sidonia, taken ill on Maundy Thursday, died the day after Easter, Tycho withdrew as the court went into mourning. They never met again, but the visit seeded the century's most celebrated astronomical correspondence, and the landgrave's later embassy to Frederik II urging support for Tycho proved decisive for the Hven endowment. Tycho's own fond memories of the stay are printed (TBOO VI, 10 and 34).

Frankfurt am Main city B 1 documented stay
Frankfurt am Main, Germany · period names: Francofurtum ad Maenum, Frankfurt am Main · 50.1109, 8.6821
Book-fair city, visited on the 1575 journey; thereafter Tycho worked the fairs only through agents and catalogues — the recurring fair-attendance claim is a phantom (nv-frankfurt-fairs).
April 1575 A
books & printingin transit
Leaving mourning Kassel in April 1575, Tycho went to Frankfurt am Main for the spring book fair. He stayed some days, turning over a great variety of books and buying not a few - above all whatever published tracts on the new star of 1572 he did not yet possess, the pamphlets he would later dissect in the Progymnasmata. Thoren reconstructs the breadth of the purchases: Proclus, pseudo-Ptolemaic astrologica, Synesius, Bonatti, recent Philippist authors, French and Italian treatises including du Chesne and five works of Oronce Fine, Gesner's bibliography, and works on mining and minerals serving the alchemical interests. The stop ties the tour to his lifelong book-buying practice - in 1579 he would send Vedel to this fair with a marked-up catalogue.

Regensburg city A 1 documented stay
Regensburg, Germany · period names: Ratisbona, Ratisbon · 49.0134, 12.1016
Imperial free city on the Danube; Tycho attended the coronation of Rudolf II as King of the Romans on 1 November 1575.
c. October 1575 – November 1575 A
court & patronagesocial visitbooks & printing
Tycho attended the Regensburg festivities for the coronation of Rudolf of Habsburg as King of the Romans, performed with great solemnity on 1 November 1575 - his first bodily crossing of the path of the prince who would become his last patron. He had hoped to find Landgrave Wilhelm, who alone among the German princes did not come; instead he met the imperial physician Thaddaeus Hagecius, and in a few days the two formed a lifelong bond: Hagecius gave him his Dialexis on the new star, Munosius's Spanish tract, and - a most precious gift - a manuscript of Copernicus's unprinted Commentariolus, which Tycho later circulated to German astronomers, reciprocating with du Chesne's new book from Frankfurt. Hugo Blotius and Gemperlin were in the company; a manuscript De directionum significationibus he examined with Hagecius here was still on his mind in 1585 (TBOO VI, 95). Soon after the coronation he started for home to prepare the intended spring emigration.

Saalfeld town A 1 documented stay
Saalfeld (Saale), Thuringia, Germany · period names: Saalfeld, Saltfeldia · 50.6500, 11.3600
Thuringian home of Erasmus Reinhold the younger, visited on the 1575 journey.
c. November 1575 B
social visitbooks & printingin transit
On the road home Tycho visited Erasmus Reinhold the Younger at Saalfeld in Thuringia - the physician-son of the calculator of the Prutenic Tables, himself author of a tract on the new star. Reinhold showed him his father's surviving manuscripts, notably the Tables enriched with planetary equations of centre (prosthaphaereses) painstakingly tabulated for every ten minutes of anomaly, and - per Christianson - the elder Reinhold's annotations in Copernicus's De revolutionibus; he also gave Tycho the Almanach Astrologicum he had compiled for the previous year, for the sake of its matter on the new star. A formative encounter with the working papers behind the tables Tycho had just been lecturing from.

Bramstedt castle-manor A 2 documented stays
Bad Bramstedt, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany · period names: Bramstedt, Bramstedt in Holstein · 53.9195, 9.8815
Heinrich Rantzau residence in Holstein; received Tycho in September 1597, was his station on 8 October 1597, and hosted the meeting with the Brandenburg party on 22 December 1597.
September 1597 – 8 October 1597 (bounds uncertain) B
court & patronagesocial visit
From Segeberg Tycho and the familia proceeded to Bramstedt, where Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau received them with open arms in the second half of September 1597. Host and guest — two of the most famous learned aristocrats of the North, friends since Tycho's Rostock student days — talked over patronage strategy and a suitable residence until a Danish restoration could be won. Under the delicate protocol of status Rantzau would not become Tycho's patron nor Tycho his client; as friend and equal he offered, of the eighteen castles and manors he and his sons owned, Wandsburg near Hamburg, over the head of its lessee Georg Ludwig Frobenius, Tycho's old Hven acquaintance. Thoren has Tycho still (or again) at Bramstedt on 8 October 1597, talking over the alternatives when he sent a letter to Basel.

The sources disagree. Christianson has the Bramstedt reception in the second half of September with the caravan rolling into Wandsburg 'soon after' (late September); Thoren's 8 October 1597 Basel letter places Tycho at Bramstedt weeks later, with Wandsbek settled only mid-October — either a prolonged negotiation, or a second Bramstedt visit from Wandsburg; unresolved.
22 December 1597 A
court & patronagesocial visit
Viceroy Rantzau arranged for Tycho to meet Margrave Joachim Frederick of Brandenburg and Margravine Catherine of Brandenburg-Küstrin at Bramstedt on 22 December 1597, as the parents of Christian IV's bride returned home through Holstein from the royal wedding (Haderslev, 27 November). Tycho handed the margrave a letter and memorandum of his reasons for leaving Denmark, seeking intercession with his new royal son-in-law — either the permanent endowment of Uraniborg or leave to remove the four great instruments with compensation. The accommodating couple's letters to king and queen of January–February 1598 (25 January and days following) led to nothing. The meeting also renewed acquaintance with the Brandenburg court astrologer Johannes Müller, who had visited Hven in 1596 and would shortly join Tycho at Wandsbek.

Doberan waypoint C 1 documented stay
Bad Doberan, Germany · period names: Doberan · 54.1069, 11.9050
Mecklenburg; the fief pledged for Tycho's loan to the young dukes; probable stop on the westward road from Rostock, Sept 1597. The claimed loan-delivery journey is a phantom (nv-doberan-loan).
c. 8 September 1597 – September 1597 C
in transitproperty
Leaving Rostock on 8 September 1597, the Brahe caravan proceeded westward through Doberan on the coastal road toward Wismar and Holstein — a pointed waypoint, since the whole Amt of Doberan had just been pledged as surety for Tycho's 10,000-daler loan to the young Mecklenburg dukes. Having refused to pay the sum out at Wismar, Tycho had offered to deliver it at Doberan in person, 'which probably happened' in Norlind's hedged wording; Friis, however, records only the promise, never the execution — and in 1601 it was Eske Bille and his servant, not Tycho, who travelled to Doberan and Rostock for the repayment. The passage is a named route stage in Christianson; no halt or business is independently documented.

Segeberg castle-manor B 1 documented stay
Siegesburg fortress, Bad Segeberg, Germany · period names: Segeberg · 53.9400, 10.3100
Fortress on the Kalkberg, official seat of Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau; among the refuges Rantzau offered Tycho in 1597.
17 September 1597 A
in transitcourt & patronageexile
By 17 September 1597 the exile party had reached Segeberg fortress, seat of Viceroy Heinrich Rantzau's administration of royal Schleswig-Holstein — one of the castles Rantzau had offered — only to find the viceroy away at Bramstedt. From Segeberg Tycho wrote him the dated letter (TBOO VIII,5) that fixes his presence: the castle pleased him, but he had left Hven to relocate, not retire — he had books to finish and needed typographic equipment, engravers and printers, so he asked for a residence near a city like Hamburg or Lübeck and offered to come to Bramstedt to discuss plans. That criterion shortly selected Wandsburg. Thoren's 'first estate, too remote for his taste', from which the 17 September letter was sent, is this same station, not a separate unnamed castle.

Wandsbek castle-manor A 1 documented stay
Wandsbek (Wandsburg castle site), Hamburg, Germany · period names: Wandesburgum, Wandesburg, Wandsburg, Wandesbeck · 53.5730, 10.0700
Heinrich Rantzau's moated castle on the northern outskirts of Hamburg; Tycho's exile seat 1597-98 and the imprint place of the Mechanica (1598).
The castle is demolished (1861, per Norlind); nothing of it stands.
October 1597 – 29 September 1598cal. A
exilebooks & printingcourt & patronageobservationinstrumentsalchemy & medicine
A year as Rantzau's guest — not client — at the moated castle of Wandsburg in Wandsbek on Hamburg's outskirts, living in quasi-princely style, honoured at church in a special loge. Christian IV's rebuff of 8 October 1597 reached him here; on 20 October he entered the account of his interrupted observations and composed the Elegia ad Daniam, and on 21 October resumed observing, at first with only a radius, from February 1598 with quadrants, sextant and armilla (pole height 53°36'; lunar eclipse 10 February with Rosenkrantz assisting, solar eclipse 25 February, lunar 6 August). His own press from Hven, worked by the Hamburg printer Philipp von Ohr, produced the Astronomiae instauratae mechanica (dedication to Rudolf II dated 31 December 1597, ready early 1598), while copyists lettered vellum exemplars of the 1,000-star catalogue; both went out to princes and scholars across Europe as the patronage suit which, brokered by Rantzau, Hagecius, Corraducius and the Elector of Cologne, produced the imperial invitation in the summer. He kept a laboratory, shared medical recipes with Rantzau, answered Kepler's Mysterium on 1 April 1598, and received a stream of Danish students, Müller, Fabricius and, from August 1598, Longomontanus. Day-dated letters and album leaves run from 2 January to 14 September 1598. Just after Michaelmas, 29 September 1598, the caravan rolled out toward the Elbe road.

The sources disagree. Arrival: late September 1597 (Christianson 2000 p.220; 2020 'within the month' of 8 Sept) vs about mid-October (Dreyer p.266, Thoren p.381, Friis p.246, Björklund p.117, Bøggild-Johannsen) — mid-October adopted as the settlement date, supported by Thoren's 8 October Bramstedt letter; Frobenius found Tycho installed by 15 October (Christianson p.285). The Elegia ad Daniam: written at Wandsbek 20 October 1597 (Dreyer, Thoren, Christianson 2020, Björklund) vs Christianson 2000's vague 'later that same year'. Norlind doubts Christian IV personally composed the 8 October 1597 answer (a Saturday; the king had the letter only 'this week'). Christianson 2020 narrates the Brandenburg-electors meeting without a place inside his 1598 sequence — it belongs to Bramstedt, 22 December 1597.
Dresden city A 2 documented stays
Dresden, Germany · period names: Dresden, Dresda · 51.0502, 13.7376
Electoral Saxon residence city on the Elbe; single-day album evidence 10 November 1598, and a named station ('til Dresden') on the June 1599 journey to Bohemia.
October 1598 – December 1598 (bounds uncertain)cal. A
in transitcourt & patronage
Tycho, his sons, Tengnagel and a small suite spent about a month in the Electoral Saxon residence city (late October to the first days of December 1598). He announced his approach to the imperial court through Vice-Chancellor Corraducius; the round trip of the inquiry took a month, Prague being gripped by plague and Rudolf withdrawn (to Pilsen, per Björklund's Bilag 4). Secretary Barvitius's reply — the emperor was pleased he was on the way but he should wait at a safe distance — turned him to wintering at Wittenberg. In Dresden he had an audience with Duke Frederick William of Saxe-Altenburg, administrator of Electoral Saxony, presenting illuminated copies of the Mechanica and star catalogue to the duke, the boy Elector Christian II and Chancellor Mosbach, and receiving a golden chain with three portrait medallions worth over 130 gulden. From Dresden on 28 November 1598 he dated the letter to the Doge of Venice — carried by Tengnagel across the Alps, proposing among other things the affiliate observatory at Alexandria — and wrote Magini after a seven-year silence. His son Tycho was sent back to Wandsbek to fetch the family.

16 June 1599 – June 1599cal. A
in transitfamily
The Dresden split of the household. Arriving on 16 June 1599, two days out of Wittenberg, Tycho left Kirsten, the daughters and their servants in the care of Johann Tauchmann, a high Saxon court official and brother-in-law of his Wittenberg collaborator Jöstelius, and went on toward Prague in his finest carriage with his sons and Claus Mule — a deliberate strategy of appearing before the emperor unencumbered, and of holding a line of retreat. On imperial instructions after the first audience the family was fetched, reaching Prague eight days after being sent for.

Magdeburg city B 1 documented stay
Magdeburg, Germany · period names: Magdeburg · 52.1300, 11.6300
Elbe city and Tycho's instrument depot 1598-1600. He was bodily here in October 1598, when the travel plan changed and the household turned back; the later winter-1599-1600 and 1600-transport presence claims are phantoms (nv-magdeburg-1599-1600).
October 1598 A
in transitcourt & patronagepropertysocial visit
The caravan progressed up the Elbe to Magdeburg and halted about eight days in October 1598. Tycho met his long-time correspondent Rector Georg Rollenhagen — source of the first warnings of Ursus's plagiarism and of imperial-court intelligence via Caspar Lehmann, including the rumour that Rudolf meant to grant him Brandeis castle. Erik Lange, Sophie Brahe's absconded betrothed, turned up: Tycho barred him and his gold-making schemes from the Prague party, but before a summoned notary required his sworn public testimony on Ursus's 1584 conduct at Uraniborg — ammunition for the plagiarism war. Strategy changed here: the heavy instruments and baggage were stored at Magdeburg (they stayed until 1600), and Longomontanus escorted Kirsten and the daughters back to Wandsburg — prospects being too uncertain to drag the whole household on — while Tycho, his sons, Tengnagel and a few others pressed on toward Dresden.

Harburg court B 1 documented stay
Harburg (Hamburg-Harburg), Germany · period names: Harburg · 53.4600, 9.9800
Ducal seat of Otto II of Braunschweig-Lüneburg on the Elbe opposite Hamburg; visited during the 1597-98 exile.
5 October 1598 A
in transitcourt & patronage
First call of the Prague journey: the caravan — three splendid carriages, Tycho's drawn by six horses, out of Wandsburg just after Michaelmas — crossed to the ducal seat of Harburg on the Elbe's south bank, where Tycho paid his respects to the aged Duke Otto II of Braunschweig-Lüneburg, whose daughter Duchess Elisabeth was married to Tycho's Swedish kinsman Count Erik Brahe. He presented an illuminated copy of the Mechanica bound in green silk, inscribed 5 October 1598; the fascinated duke asked for his nativity and reciprocated with a letter of recommendation to the imperial High Steward Wolfgang Rumpf — a document Tycho would produce at his Prague audience the next summer, alongside the commendations of Elector Ernest and Duke Ulrich.

Pretzsch castle-manor A 1 documented stay
Pretzsch (Elbe), Saxony-Anhalt, Germany · period names: Castle Pretzsch, Pretzsch · 51.7150, 12.8040

14 June 1599 – 15 June 1599cal. A
in transitsocial visit
First halt of the definitive move to Bohemia. Leaving Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 with the whole familia — a train of wagons, carriages and outriders — Tycho spent the first evening at Castle Pretzsch on the Elbe as guest of the Saxon hereditary marshal Johann (Hans) Löser, a courtesy the recently money-humbled astronomer thought worth recording for Rosenkrantz. The party continued upriver toward Dresden the next day.

Swiss & Italian journey

Basel university A 2 documented stays
Basel, Switzerland · period names: Basilea, Basilea Rauracorum · 47.5596, 7.5886
University city on the Rhine; Tycho matriculated autumn 1568 and in 1575 secretly chose it as his intended place of emigration before the Hven offer.
c. September 1568 – 1569 A
educationinstruments
By September 1568 Tycho was in Basel — city of Erasmus and Paracelsus, the university Peder Oxe had known in youth and exile — where he matriculated with cousins and several other Danes under the rectorate of Simon Sulzer, probably in August or September (standing no. 52 in the year's list). After nine years of university work he had exhausted teachers and texts: here he first worked on his own, experimenting with quadrant construction assisted by the young Hugo Blotius, later imperial librarian in Vienna — probably including the gilt brass quadrant with Nonnian subdivisions and 'an emblem of life and death' later depicted in the Mechanica, though a larger design of 1–1.5 m radius proved unstable in wind. Basel lodged itself in his affections: in 1575 he would seriously consider settling there for good. He stayed through the winter, leaving for the Danube road at the end of 1568 or in early spring 1569.
PeopleHugo Blotiusfellow student, assistant in the quadrant experiments; later imperial librarian in Vienna and intermediary to KeplerSimon Sulzerrector during matriculation (1 May 1568 – 30 April 1569)

c. 1575 A
in transiteducationother
Continuing southwest from Frankfurt, Tycho stayed some time at Basel and found it so agreeable that he resolved to settle there or nearby with his family: pure clear air and cheap living, an academy full of distinguished men in the Erasmian tradition, and above all the city's position at the meeting-point of Germany, France and Italy, whence his findings could spread and correspondence flow. Gassendi's funeral-oration source confirms that, returning homeward, he had fixed on 'Basileam Rauracorum, aut vicinum aliquem locum' as the chosen seat of his life. He deferred the final decision but carried the secret plan home at year's end - the private agenda that shaped the whole sequel, since Frederick II's offer of Hven in February 1576 was designed to forestall exactly this emigration.

Innsbruck waypoint C 1 documented stay
Innsbruck, Austria · period names: Innsbruck · 47.2700, 11.3950
Waypoint north of the Brenner Pass on the probable 1575 route to Venice.
c. 1575 C
in transit
On the return from Venice Tycho crossed the Brenner Pass before the fall snows made it uncertain and 'slipped through to Innsbruck', travelling a few days north to Augsburg - a pure transit waypoint in Thoren's account. Norlind holds the much-travelled Brenner road (Innsbruck, Trento, Treviso - the road Montaigne took five years later) to be the probable route of the outward journey as well, and the homeward journey probably retraced it. Trento and Treviso remain probable-route conjecture without any documented stop.

Jonsson holds it 'hogst troligt' (highly probable) that Tycho visited the botanical garden at Padua on the return from Venice in 1575: the fourfold garden he later laid out around Uraniborg came to resemble the Paduan plan. The claim is offered as a strong probability explaining the garden design, not as a documented visit, and Christianson expressly warns that Paduan side-trips must not be asserted since Tycho recorded no details. Rendered as an unproven probability.

Venice city B 1 documented stay
Venice, Italy · period names: Venetia, Venetiae, Venedig · 45.4408, 12.3155
The southernmost point Tycho ever reached, on the 1575 journey; its aristocratic-academy sociability shaped the Uraniborg ideal. The late-career Venetian relocation claim is a phantom (nv-venice-late-career).
c. 1575 A
social visitin transitcourt & patronage
Crossing the Alps from Basel, Tycho reached Venice - the farthest south he ever travelled - and stayed from some days to a few weeks. His own testimony survives (Progymnasmata; TBOO III, 234): about sixteen years on he recalled hearing very many Venetians, including men of the highest nobility, disputing acutely on lofty philosophical matters - words Norlind reads as attendance at the patrician learned academies, held in palaces such as the Morosini. He admired the 'splendid and grand' city, 'the Emporium of all Europe', and its most prudent government; saw the new Renaissance architecture of the Veneto, above all Palladio's, which fed directly into the Uraniborg villa ideal; and as Frederick II's agent made contacts among Venetian artisans for the Elsinore works. More than twenty years later he sent the Republic and Doge Grimani each a Mechanica with the manuscript star catalogue.

Rudolf II's imperial capital; Tycho's final court station 1599-1601, death and burial place. The constituent micro-sites (Hradčany, Golden Griffin, Curtius house, Belvedere, Týn Church) are carried as sites, not places. From Benátky he came 'rarely, except when called by the Emperor'.

The Church of Our Lady before Týn on Prague's Old Town Square, where Tycho was buried on 4 November 1601. June 1599 – August 1599cal. A
court & patronageexileobservationinstruments
Arrival in Bohemia and the making of the imperial appointment. Reaching Prague in late June or the first days of July 1599 — Ursus fleeing the city at his approach — Tycho was greeted by the privy secretary Barvitius, received by High Steward Rumpf in long Latin conversation, and granted a wholly private audience by Rudolf II, who took his hand, accepted the three presentation volumes (the Mechanica, the vellum star catalogue, the sun-and-moon theory) and promised 3,000 gulden yearly with a hereditary fief to follow. He was lodged in the late vice-chancellor Curtius's house on Hradčany, where a painted pedestal in the Uraniborg manner was built; he signed the von Wicken album at Prague on 13 July; he observed the 22 July solar eclipse with his own instruments while his assistant watched from the Carolinum tower, and his Prague solar series ends 31 July. Finding the Curtius tower too small and dreading visitors, he asked for a country seat and was offered three castles.

social visitin transit
The Kepler reconciliation. About three weeks after Kepler's angry departure from Benátky on 6 April 1600 and his withdrawal to Baron Hoffmann's house in Prague, Hoffmann's and Jessenius's mediation and Kepler's repentant letter brought the two astronomers together at Prague: Tycho drove into the city — something he had told Kepler he did not like to do — was reconciled with his errant assistant, and fetched him back to Benátky, where Kepler worked a further four weeks before leaving for Graz at the beginning of June.

c. 1 May 1600 A
social visit
At the beginning of May 1600, while resident at Benátky, Tycho attended Caspar von Mühlstein's wedding in Prague — a sign of cordial relations with the estates' captain after the December 1599 settlement of their funding frictions. Tycho's own letter of 15 May 1600 dates it: 'wie ich fur 14 tage zu Prage, auf des Herrn Haubtmans von Brandeis Hochzeit gewesen'. In this period he grew acquainted with Protestant aristocrats including Baron Ehrenfried von Minckwitz, who blazoned the same arms as his Ulfstand grandmother, and Baron Siegfried von Rindscheid, the alchemist who had visited Uraniborg with Erik Lange in 1584.

June 1600 – 24 October 1601 (bounds uncertain)cal. A
court & patronageobservationbooks & printingfamilyinstrumentsdeath & burial
The final residence. Summoned when Rudolf II returned from Pilsen on 10 June 1600, Tycho moved to Prague suddenly and permanently: first weeks in the noisy Golden Griffin inn on Nový Svět below the castle (twice summoned to the palace in one day), then a private house near Baron Hoffmann's by the Loreto square. The twenty-eight instruments — from Benátky, and the great ones from Hven via the Magdeburg transit dispute — arrived by October-November 1600 and were installed at the Belvedere; the press resumed the Progymnasmata; Jacob Monaw brought the Wittich library's annotated De revolutionibus copies in October 1600, and Kepler, expelled from Styria, returned destitute on 19 October 1600 and was set to refuting Ursus. On 25 February 1601 the household moved into the Curtius house, bought by the emperor. Elisabeth married Tengnagel on 17 June 1601; in September 1601 Tycho presented Kepler to the emperor and the Tabulae Rudolphinae were named. His last observation is dated 11 October 1601; the Rožmberk banquet of 13 October began the fatal illness, and he died at home on 24 October 1601, aged 54 years 10 months, charging Kepler to complete the tables in the Tychonic scheme.

The sources disagree. Start of the permanent Prague residence: June 1600 on Rudolf's 10 June return (Thoren, Christianson 2000/2020, Jönsson) vs 'about the beginning of July' (Norlind, from the 3 August postscript 'called a month ago') vs 'about August' (Dreyer) — June followed (modern consensus); Friis's datelines bracket it 15 May - 26 September 1600, his 26 July 'In eil, Prag' letter possibly the move itself. Death date: 24 October 1601 unanimous against Kepler's '24 November' slip (Gassendi's refutation) and the older '13 October old style' (Studnicka's correction: 13 October n.s. is the banquet). Time of death: 'around nine that evening' (Christianson 2020) vs 'between nine and ten in the forenoon' (Jönsson) vs morning (Friis, Dreyer) — morning better attested. Elisabeth's wedding: 17 June 1601 (Thoren, Jönsson, Christianson) vs Friis's 'between Easter and Pentecost 1601'. Cause of death: uraemia from prostatic hypertrophy (Norlind; modern opinion per Thoren; Christianson via Jessenius) vs the contemporary stone attribution (Wittich; no stones found at exhumation); per the Debunked Claims Register, mercury poisoning is excluded by the 2010 exhumation and uraemia is consistent but unproven — Christianson 2000's 'body heavy with quicksilver from Paracelsian elixirs' is not carried as fact. Norlind judges the Capuchin-protocol account of Tycho's court role 'extremely tendentious and certainly historically false in most points'.
2 December 1600 – February 1601 (bounds uncertain)cal. B · site record →
observationinstruments
Surrogate Uraniborg. In the Royal Summer Palace of Queen Anna — the Belvedere, 'non longe ab Arce in Caesaris quadam magnifice exstructa domo' in Tycho's report of 24 January 1601 — his twenty-eight instruments, arrived in Prague in October–November 1600 (Thoren: sometime in October, a few weeks after the Magdeburg consignment), were stored and mounted on the second-storey porch, and on 2 December 1600 the observations broken off at Benátky at the end of June were resumed; by Christmas night Tycho was observing. Pierre Bergeron (1607) records that the great Danish mathematician made his precise observations in the ground-floor arcaded galleries — reported rather than firmly documented for Tycho's own person. After his death the building housed the astronomical section of Rudolf's collections, a memorial musaeum with two portraits of Tycho.

25 February 1601 – 24 October 1601cal. A · site record →
court & patronageobservationfamilydeath & burial
Last workplace and deathplace. On 25 February 1601 the familia moved into the refurbished summer palace of the late vice-chancellor Jacob Kurz von Senftenau (Curtius) on Hradčany, bought by the emperor for 10,000 thaler and transformed toward a 'New Imperial Uraniborg'; observing resumed there on 3 March 1601, seven teams having taken the solar culmination simultaneously on 28 February. Elisabeth Brahe married Tengnagel in the house in June 1601; the Pruskowski Mechanica dedication of 12 March 1601, among the latest securely-dated Tycho autographs, was signed in this residence. After the banquet of 13 October Tycho returned here unable to pass water and died on 24 October 1601, Kirsten, Kepler and the household about him, Longomontanus and Tengnagel far from Prague. The Bohemian royal astronomer Alois David fixed the observation tower's coordinates in 1803; the structure was demolished in 1804.

13 October 1601cal. A · site record →
social visit
The fatal banquet. On 13 October 1601 Tycho went with the councillor Ehrenfried von Minckwitz to dine at the palace of Petr Vok z Rožmberka — by Thoren's reckoning (Appendix 5) the Renaissance palace on Hradčany square later known as the Schwarzenberg palace — a magnate of his bookish Prague circle, owner of some 10,000 books and manuscripts. Forbearing, as manners required while his host remained at table, to rise and relieve himself, he held his urine too long; by the time he returned home he could not urinate, and the eleven-day fatal illness began. The retention story is the contemporary tradition transmitted by Kepler's log and the funeral oration, not an established medical fact.

4 November 1601cal. A · site record →
death & burial
The burial. On 4 November 1601 a solemn procession bore the coffin — velvet-covered, hung with his ancestors' gilded arms, preceded by the black damask banner with his title, his led horse and gilt rapier — across the Charles Bridge along the royal way to the Church of Our Lady before Týn in the Old Town, where the utraquist rite still allowed a Protestant service. Twelve noble imperial guardsmen carried him; his younger son Jørgen walked between Count Erik Brahe and Baron von Minckwitz, the widow following; the eldest son and son-in-law Tengnagel were abroad. Jessenius delivered the funeral oration, printed at Prague the same year. The red Slivenec marble monument — armoured effigy, hand on the celestial globe, 'NON FASCES, NEC OPES, SOLA ARTIS SCEPTRA PERENNANT' — still marks the tomb, where Kirsten was laid beside him in 1604. (This final entry records the burial rite of 4 November — Tycho died on 24 October; it closes the itinerary as the body's last journey, not a living presence.)

Benátky nad Jizerou — Tycho's first Bohemian observatory extant B 1599–1600
The hilltop castle at Benátky nad Jizerou, about 30 km north of Prague, granted to Tycho by Rudolf II in 1599 as his first Bohemian observatory — high on a hill with a commanding view, an astronomer's choice. He was given leave to build wooden observing cubicles (now vanished); the portion available to him ran to three floors of nearly 500 m² each. 20 August 1599 – June 1600 (bounds uncertain)cal. A · site record →
observationinstrumentsalchemy & medicinecourt & patronagefamilyproperty
The last observatory. Choosing Benátky nad Jizerou — highest of the three offered crown estates, c. 35 km northeast of Prague above the 'Venice of Bohemia' — Tycho arrived about 20-21 August 1599, had his first instrument mounted by 28 August, and set about remodelling the castle into a new Uraniborg with observatory and chymical laboratory, against the obstruction of the administrator Mühlstein and an empty treasury (imperial resolution of 10 December 1599: 1,000 gulden yearly from the Brandeis-Benátky rents). His first recorded observation there is 11 September 1599; datelines run 'from the imperial castle Benatky' from 7 September 1599 to 15 May 1600. Son Tycho and Claus Mule fetched the great instruments from Denmark; Longomontanus rejoined in January 1600 for the lunar theory; Kepler first met him here on 3 February 1600 and was set to Mars, the contract quarrel mediated by Jessenius on 5 April. David Gans came thrice from Prague, five days each. Observations break off at the end of June 1600, when the emperor recalled him to Prague.

The sources disagree. Departure for Prague: observations end at the end of June 1600 (Studnicka; Christianson 2020 has the household leave after Rudolf's 10 June return) vs early July (Norlind) vs c. August on Barvitius's advice (Dreyer); June followed as the modern consensus, with Friis's dateline gap (15 May 1600 Benátky - 26 September 1600 Prague) bracketing it. Kepler's arrival: 3 February 1600 (Dreyer, McEvoy in Crossroads) vs 4 February summons (Christianson 2020) vs 'January to Prague' (Jönsson, outlier) — 3 February followed. Longomontanus's discharge: 18 July 1600 at Benátky (Christianson 2000) vs 4 August / August 1600 (Christianson 2020, Friis, Norlind, Dreyer). The Hamburg-senate letter's two internal datings (29 Sep 1599 slug vs '27 jan. n.s. Benatky') disagree; both place Tycho at Benátky in 1599-1600. Jönsson places Benátky 'southwest' of Prague — a geographical error; the castle lies northeast.

Imperial hunting-lodge on the Elbe, administrative seat of the Benátky-Brandeis crown estates. Tycho datelined a letter here 20 Aug 1599 (n.s.) and inspected the castle, but declined it as a residence — see the phantom register (nv-brandys-residence).
20 August 1599 – 21 August 1599cal. A
in transitproperty
Seen on the castle-selection circuit and passed over — sitting low, the Emperor's favourite hunting-lodge — Brandeis nonetheless anchors the removal to Benátky: on the way there Tycho datelined a letter to Longomontanus at Rostock from Brandeis, 20 August 1599 (new style), reporting a level road about six hours from Prague and that an official of Brandeis would carry him and all his effects to Benátky that day or the next. Brandeis remained the administrative seat, under Kaspar von Mühlstein, from which his Benátky building funds were grudgingly managed. He never resided here.

Plague refuge November-December 1599; the jicice cluster (Christianson 2020) is merged here — same refuge, different spelling.
November 1599 – January 1600 B
otherobservationin transit
Plague refuge. After two thousand deaths in the Benátky district — a travelling companion of the visiting cousin Claus Steensen Bille sickened and died on arrival — Tycho took the frightened household to the castle of Girsitz in the first half of November 1599. He said they stayed six or seven weeks: his first letter from Girsitz is of 16 November, the last officially sent from there of 31 December 1599, with the return to Benátky in the new year; some intervening letters were addressed from Benátky 'just to avoid complicating things', so the exact return is unfixable. Some observations were made in December, and during this visitation the Emperor asked Tycho for the prescription of his elixir against epidemic diseases.

Duration: Christianson confines the refuge to November-December 1599; Thoren and Norlind extend the return into the new year — the 31 December last letter supports a January 1600 return.

The journeys

Documented route sequences — only the stations the sources name, in the order the evidence supports; where the accounts differ, the dispute is stated, not smoothed over.
14 February 1562 – 24 March 1562 First study journey: Copenhagen to Leipzig, February–March 1562 A
Copenhagen → Wittenberg → Leipzig
Departed Copenhagen 14 February 1562, arrived Leipzig 24 March — five and a half weeks by ship across the southern Baltic, then on horseback along the Elbe and Saale, passing through Wittenberg and riding two more days to Leipzig. Wittenberg is the only intermediate station any source names; Dreyer, Friis, Norlind, Jönsson and Christianson 2020 name none. Kinsmen had arranged a good reception in Leipzig in advance.

17 May 1565 – June 1565 Return from Leipzig to wartime Denmark, May–June 1565 A
Leipzig → Wittenberg → Rostock → Copenhagen → Helsingborg → Malmö → Knutstorp
The best-dated of the early journeys: Tycho and Vedel left Leipzig on 17 May 1565 (Hegelund's date), passed through Wittenberg, reached Rostock on 25 May (Stephanius), and crossed the war-time Baltic to Copenhagen without meeting hostile cruisers, the Danish and Swedish fleets massing in the Sound. The onward legs — Copenhagen, Helsingborg, Malmö, Knutstorp, with latitude determinations under way — are Norlind's probable reading of the pole-height list in the oldest observation journal. Gassendi has a direct sail from Rostock to the fatherland.

The Scanian waypoints rest on the journal inference; Gassendi has the ship sail 'recta in patriam' from Rostock. A parallel stationless record of the same return (Jönsson: probably at Jørgen Brahe's urging; Christianson 2020: home in late May) was merged here.
April 1566 – 15 April 1566 Second departure: Denmark to Wittenberg, April 1566 A
Knutstorp → Wittenberg
Early in 1566 Tycho left Denmark for the second time — without a noble hovmester, in the company of the M.A. Hans Aalborg and at least one other Dane — arriving at Wittenberg on 15 April 1566 (Stephanius: 'Returned to Wittenberg on April 15, 1566, from his fatherland'). Gassendi frames the departure as hastened 'not without a show of anger' at his relations' contempt for his studies.

An epidemic emptied the congested little university town: Tycho and Aalborg left Wittenberg on 16 September 1566 and reached Rostock on 24 September, 'fleeing on account of the plague' (Stephanius), an eight-day journey; he matriculated at Rostock the following month.

After his twenty-first birthday and the Christmas holidays at home, Tycho embarked on his third trip abroad, arriving at Rostock on 1 January 1568 — this time entirely without a tutor, amid friction with his father over the direction of his studies.

During 1568 — under the shadow of the unpaid duel fine, and freed from law by the canonry promise — Tycho travelled south across Germany, purchasing instruments at Nuremberg (Christianson 2020), and was matriculated at Basel by the autumn. The exact route is otherwise unrecorded: Thoren allows a possible meeting with his brother Steen at Arnstadt for the dubbing by Count Günther of Schwarzburg, and a 'perhaps Wittenberg' — both too hedged to log as stays. The traditional intermediate Wittenberg residence (Gassendi, Dreyer, Friis) is rejected by Norlind.

December 1568 – 14 April 1569 Basel to Augsburg by the Danube road, early 1569 B
Basel → Freiburg im Breisgau → Lauingen → Ingolstadt → Augsburg
Leaving Basel at the turn of 1568/69, Tycho turned the road to Augsburg into a tour of south-German astronomical practitioners: Schreckenfuchs's planetary models at Freiburg, the night-long dinner with Leovitius at Lauingen, and (on Norlind's redating) the call on Philip Apian at Ingolstadt, reaching Augsburg in time to observe from 14 April 1569.

16 May 1570 – 30 December 1570 Homeward from Augsburg to Helsingborg, May–December 1570 A
Augsburg → Wittenberg → Rostock → Helsingborg
An unhurried homecoming whose route, previously unknown, is partly fixed by Norlind's find: last Quadrans Maximus observation at Augsburg 16 May 1570; the Textor album leaf proving Wittenberg on 9 September 1570; probably a call on the Rostock professors (Thoren); across the Baltic; and observing at Helsingborg Castle by 30 December 1570, the sextant and unfinished globe left in Paul Hainzel's keeping at Augsburg. The older tradition routed him through Ingolstadt with a Copenhagen landfall; the motive — his father's illness — is itself questioned.

January 1574 – May 1574 The early-1574 Skane-Oresund observing circuit C
Knutstorp → Herrevad Abbey → Copenhagen
The compiler's continuous itinerary sentence has Tycho at the start of 1574 on his Skane estates, observing at Herrevad Abbey in March and April (Dreyer, from the same books, extends the run into May), and in Copenhagen from late April and May, where he mostly lived for the rest of the year. The compiler also places him on Hven on 22 February 1574 'af hvad Anledning vides ikke'; that leg is excluded here because Dreyer showed the observed Mars-moon conjunction fits 22 February 1576, not 1574 - the first documented Hven visit therefore falls outside this period.

The sources disagree. The compiler (after Langebek, Danske Magazin ii. 194) has Tycho on Hven with observations on 22 February 1574; Dreyer (printed p. 86 n.) refutes the dating - on that day the moon was a few days old and Mars on the other side of the heavens, whereas the observed close Mars-moon conjunction fits 22 February 1576 exactly. The Hven leg is excluded from the route; the first Hven visit belongs to 1576 (per-6).
March 1575 – December 1575 The grand tour of 1575 A
Copenhagen → Kassel → Frankfurt am Main → Basel → Venice → Innsbruck → Augsburg → Regensburg → Nuremberg → Saalfeld → Wittenberg → Sorø Abbey → Knutstorp
Departing about March 1575 as a grand seigneur with servants, portable instruments and probably Flemlose, Tycho went first to Kassel (late March-April, eight to ten days with Wilhelm IV), then to the Frankfurt spring book fair, southwest to Basel (the emigration target chosen), over the Alps to Venice - his farthest south - and back over the Brenner via Innsbruck to Augsburg (late summer to late October: the cracked Schissler globe, Gemperlin recruited), downriver to Regensburg for Rudolf II's coronation on 1 November (Hagecius, the Commentariolus), then home via Nuremberg (Camerarius, Labenwolf), Saalfeld (Reinhold's manuscripts) and Wittenberg (Schuler's triquetrum, the crypto-Calvinist purge), reaching the Yuletide court at Soro by December and Knutstorp for the winter. The outward order Kassel-Frankfurt-Basel-Venice and the return order Augsburg-Regensburg-Nuremberg-Saalfeld-Wittenberg are the consensus of the ordered sources; the two fixed anchors are the spring fair and the 1 November coronation.

11 February 1576 – 22 February 1576 The Ibstrup summons and Hven decision circuit, February 1576 A
Knutstorp → Ibstrup → Knutstorp → Herrevad Abbey → Copenhagen → Frederiksborg → Ven (Hven)
A fully dated circuit, documented by Tycho's own account written three days after the audience, that converted the planned Basel emigration into the Hven enterprise: the pre-dawn royal courier at Knutstorp (11 February), the same-day ride to the private audience at Ibstrup, back to Knutstorp to deliberate, consultation rides to Herrevad (Steen Bille) and Copenhagen (Pratensis, Dancay), acceptance at Frederiksborg on 18 February with the 500-daler pension, and the first crossing to Hven with its first observation on 22 February 1576.

The sources disagree. Thoren places the Herrevad and Copenhagen consultation legs in January 1576, before the summons; Christianson's mid-February ordering is followed for the route. Four per-source journey records collapsed into this one canonical circuit.
February 1597 – 11 April 1597 Final removal from Hven to Copenhagen (February–April 1597) A
Ven (Hven) → Copenhagen
The rolling evacuation of the observatory: Tycho's letter to Rantzau of 22 February 1597 — overlooked by previous biographers (Thoren) — shows the move to Copenhagen already in progress; the last Hven observation was made 15 March; the first crossing over was 18 March, the day the pension stopped; movable instruments, library, laboratory and press were boated to the Farvergade complex through the spring; and on 11 April 1597 the diary records the household's entry into the 'novum Museum Hafniense'. He never returned to the island.

2 June 1597 – June 1597 Out of Denmark: Copenhagen to Rostock (2 June – mid-June 1597) B
Copenhagen → Køge → Vordingborg → Nykøbing Falster → Gedser → Rostock
On Thursday 2 June 1597 (Julian) Tycho, Kirsten, the six children, chaplain Wensøsil, students and servants — more than a score of people, with wagons bearing library, instruments, presses, the great globe and ironbound treasure chests, under armed escort — left Copenhagen and reached Rostock by mid-June. Christianson reconstructs the southern road through Køge and Vordingborg (his foster father's boyhood castles), the Falster crossing, Nykøbing, and embarkation at Gedser; the endpoints and dates are secure, the interior stations are reconstruction. The route deliberately retraced Tycho's boyhood geography, framed by the exempla of returned exiles Peter Oxe, Knud Brahe, Erik Sparre and Erik Lange.

The sources disagree. Three incompatible route versions: (1) Christianson's overland caravan through Køge–Vordingborg–Falster–Nykøbing with the sea crossing from Gedser; (2) Norlind's 'probably over Køge and Lübeck to Rostock'; (3) a ship boarded at Copenhagen itself (Gassendi's hired cargo vessel; Jonsson; Friis 'fragtede et Skib'). The 2 June departure from Copenhagen is Tycho's own dated statement and secure; the mode and stations of the crossing are not — all three versions preserved. Gassendi's 'aestate paene media' (almost midsummer) is loose but compatible. Christianson 2000 calls 2 June a Saturday; 2 June 1597 (Julian) fell on a Thursday — the date itself, Tycho's own (Acta 124), is secure; the weekday is Christianson's slip.
8 September 1597 – October 1597 Rostock to Wandsburg via Segeberg and Bramstedt (8 September – mid-October 1597) A
Rostock → Doberan → Wismar → Segeberg → Bramstedt → Wandsbek
Fleeing the Rostock pestilence with no royal answer in hand, the familia left Rostock on 8 September 1597 and moved westward through Doberan (the Amt just pledged for Tycho's loan) and Wismar into Holstein, reaching the viceregal fortress of Segeberg by 17 September. Rantzau being at Bramstedt, Tycho wrote ahead stating his need of a residence near a printing city; at Bramstedt the viceroy received the party with open arms and lent Wandsburg over its lessee's head. The move formalised the friend-and-guest, not patron-client, relation with Rantzau. Settlement at Wandsbek followed in mid-October (Thoren, Dreyer, Friis) or late September (Christianson).
Evidence

“took their leave of Rostock on 8 September 1597 and proceeded westward through Doberan and Wismar... By 17 September, they had arrived at Segeberg Fortress”

“Invitatus ab Henrico Rantzovio omnia Wandesburgum, per Hamburgum transfert” the goods moved via Hamburg; not a bodily Hamburg stay

The sources disagree. Wandsbek settlement: late September 1597 (Christianson) vs mid-October (Dreyer, Thoren, Friis, Björklund, Bøggild-Johannsen) — mid-October adopted, with Thoren's 8 October Bramstedt letter as the hinge. Thoren's unnamed 'first estate, too remote' is identified with Segeberg (same 17 September letter). Dreyer and Friis, lacking the Holstein stations, run Rostock direct to Wandsbek in mid-October — compression, not conflict, once the September stations are admitted.
29 September 1598 – 4 December 1598 The interrupted Prague journey: Wandsburg to Wittenberg via Harburg, Magdeburg and Dresden (29 September – 4 December 1598) A
Wandsbek → Harburg → Magdeburg → Wittenberg → Dresden → Wittenberg
The first push toward Rudolf II, doubling as a patronage campaign — each halt yielded a recommendation, deposition or princely contact. Out of Wandsburg just after Michaelmas, 29 September 1598, in a caravan of three or more coaches: the Harburg call on Duke Otto II (Mechanica inscribed 5 October); about eight days at Magdeburg (Rollenhagen; Erik Lange's notarised Ursus deposition; instruments stored; Kirsten and the daughters sent back to Wandsburg with Longomontanus); up the Elbe through Wittenberg (album leaf 25 October, the Jessenius acquaintance made in passing); a month at Dresden awaiting imperial instructions (Venice and Magini letters 28 November); then, advised to defer Prague for the plague, the hundred-kilometre retreat to Wittenberg, reached 4 December 1598, for the winter.
Evidence
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), PDF pp.233-235, 302
“Just after Michaelmas... 29 September 1598... The caravan progressed as far as Magdeburg, where they stayed for a week... to Dresden, where they remained for a month.”

The sources disagree. Departure: 29 September 1598 (Christianson) vs beginning of October (Norlind, Björklund Bilag 4). Route order: the internal stores frame Wittenberg as reached c.21 October with Dresden a mid-November excursion; the biographies' Magdeburg → Dresden (month) → Wittenberg 4 December is followed, the 25 October Wittenberg leaf explained by Thoren's note that the Elbe road passed through Wittenberg. Friis and Gassendi compress the route (omitting Harburg and Magdeburg, and Dresden in Gassendi's case). The press materiel and heavy instruments travelled separately and wintered at Magdeburg, reaching Prague only in 1600 (Christianson p.337; Nielsen §1.5; Wolfschmidt: November 1600).
14 June 1599 – July 1599 Wittenberg to Prague via Pretzsch and Dresden, 14 June - early July 1599 A
Wittenberg → Pretzsch → Dresden → Prague
The definitive move to imperial service on Coraduz's summons. The whole familia left Wittenberg on 14 June 1599 — the departure self-dated in Tycho's farewell album leaf, 'quo Witebergā discessi' — spent the first night at Castle Pretzsch with Johann Löser, and reached Dresden on 16 June, where the female household was left with Johann Tauchmann. Tycho crossed the Ore Mountains with his sons and Claus Mule in his finest carriage, Ursus fleeing Prague at his approach; arrival fell in late June or the first days of July, and the von Wicken album entry of 13 July 1599 attests him at Prague within the month. The family followed from Dresden after the first audience.
Evidence
Christianson, On Tycho's Island (2000), PDF p.238
“Tycho Brahe and all his familia took leave of Wittenberg on 14 June 1599... He proceeded on to Prague in his finest carriage with his son, Tycho Tygesen, and a few servants.”

“They left right after summer solstice, traveling en masse to Dresden... On arriving there 'about the beginning of July'”

“Den 14 juni 1599 g.st. bröt Tycho upp från Wittenberg till Prag”
Friis, Tyge Brahe (1871), Friis 1871 p. 265 (PDF 277)
“Tyge Brahe begav sig nu paa Reisen dertil strax efter Paaske 1599, og han lagde Veien over Dresden”
